challenge.q: Read a whole number and print it reversed as a number (1230 prints 321). Use math, not strings.
challenge.solution:
n = int(input())
rev = 0
while n > 0:
    rev = rev * 10 + n % 10
    n //= 10
print(rev)

units.title: Working with Text
units.blurb: Slice, search, clean and transform text, the raw material of most real programs.

ex.title: Every character has a position
ex.text:
Positions (indexes) start at **0**. Negative indexes count from the end: `-1` is the last character.
A **slice** `s[start:stop]` takes characters from start up to (not including) stop. Leave a side empty to go to the edge. `s[::-1]` reverses.
ex.code:
word = "python"
print(word[0], word[-1])
print(word[1:4])
print(word[:2], word[2:])
print(word[::-1])
print(len(word))

s = "keyboard"
print(s[3:6])
ex.why: Positions 3, 4 and 5 are b, o, a.

ex.code: print("hello"[-2])

ex.q: Strings can't be changed in place. What does `s[0] = "J"` do?
opts: It adds J at the start
ex.why: Strings are immutable. Build a new one instead, like "J" + s[1:].

ex.q: Read a full name like `Ada Lovelace` and print the initials, like `A.L.`
ex.solution:
name = input()
space = name.index(" ")
print(name[0] + "." + name[space + 1] + ".")
hints: name.index(" ") gives the position of the space.

ex.q: Read a word and print `palindrome` if it reads the same backwards (ignoring capitals), otherwise `not a palindrome`.

ex.title: Built-in text tools
ex.text:
Strings come with methods (functions you call with a dot):
- `.lower()` `.upper()` `.title()` change case
- `.strip()` trims spaces from both ends
- `.replace(old, new)` swaps text
- `.find(x)` gives the position of x (or −1), `.count(x)` counts it
- `.startswith(x)` `.endswith(x)` and `x in s` check for text
They return **new** strings; the original doesn't change.
ex.code:
raw = "   Hello, World   "
clean = raw.strip()
print(clean.lower())
print(clean.replace("World", "Python"))
print(clean.count("l"), clean.find("W"), "World" in clean)
print("banana".count("an"))
ex.why: "an" appears at positions 1 and 3.

ex.code:
email = "  Sam@Example.COM "
print(email.strip().lower())

ex.q: Clean up a username: read it, trim spaces, make it lowercase and replace spaces inside with underscores. `  Grace Hopper ` becomes `grace_hopper`.
ex.solution: print(input().strip().lower().replace(" ", "_"))

ex.q: Read an email address. Print `valid` if it contains exactly one `@`, has a `.` after the @, and doesn't start or end with `@`. Otherwise print `invalid`.

ex.title: Formatting like a pro
ex.text: f-strings can align text in columns. `{name:<10}` pads to 10 characters, left-aligned. `>` aligns right, `^` centers. Numbers combine it: `{price:>8.2f}`.

ex.title: One character at a time
ex.text: `for ch in text:` visits each character. Combine it with checks like `ch.isdigit()`, `ch.isalpha()`, `ch.isupper()` or `ch in "aeiou"`.

ex.q: Read a sentence and print how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u, upper or lower case) it has.
Read a word and print it reversed, without using slicing. Build the result one character at a time.
ex.solution:
word = input()
rev = ""
for ch in word:
    rev = ch + rev
print(rev)

ex.q: Password check: read a password and print `strong` only if it's at least 8 characters and has at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter and one digit. Otherwise print `weak`.
Run-length encoding squeezes repeats: `aaabccdddd` becomes `a3b1c2d4`. Read a string and print its encoding.
ex.solution:
s = input()
out = ""
i = 0
while i < len(s):
    j = i
    while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:
        j += 1
    out += s[i] + str(j - i)
    i = j
print(out)
hints: Find where each run of the same letter ends, then add the letter and the run length.

ex.title: ord() and chr()
ex.text:
Every character has a number code. `ord("A")` is 65, `ord("a")` is 97. `chr(66)` turns a code back into "B".
That makes it easy to shift letters: the heart of every simple cipher.
ex.code:
print(ord("A"), ord("Z"), ord("a"))
print(chr(72) + chr(105))
print(chr(ord("c") + 1))
print(chr(ord("x") + 2))

ex.title: Wrapping around
ex.text:
To shift "z" forward by 1 and land on "a", convert the letter to 0–25, add the shift, wrap with `% 26`, then convert back.
`chr((ord(ch) - ord("a") + shift) % 26 + ord("a"))`
ex.code:
shift = 3
for ch in "xyz":
    print(chr((ord(ch) - ord("a") + shift) % 26 + ord("a")), end="")
print()

ex.q: ROT13 shifts every letter by 13 (and works the same way to decode). Read a lowercase message and print it with every letter shifted by 13. Leave spaces and other characters as they are.

challenge.code: print("abcdef"[1::2])
print("Mississippi".replace("ss", "S").count("S"))

challenge.q: Read a sentence and print the number of words in it (words are separated by single spaces, ignore leading and trailing spaces).
challenge.solution:
s = input().strip()
print(0 if s == "" else s.count(" ") + 1)

challenge.q: Read a word and print it with each letter's case swapped, without using .swapcase(). `PyThOn` becomes `pYtHoN`.
challenge.solution:
out = ""
for ch in input():
    out += ch.lower() if ch.isupper() else ch.upper()
print(out)

challenge.q: Read two words and print `anagram` if they use exactly the same letters (ignoring case), otherwise `not anagram`. `Listen` and `Silent` are anagrams.
challenge.solution:
a = input().lower()
b = input().lower()
print("anagram" if sorted(a) == sorted(b) else "not anagram")

units.title: Functions
units.blurb: Package code into reusable tools with names, inputs and outputs. This is how real programs are organized.

ex.title: def
ex.text:
A **function** is a named block of code you can run whenever you want. `def` defines it; calling it with `()` runs it.
Functions let you write something once and use it everywhere, and give the idea a name.
ex.code:
def banner():
    print("=" * 20)
    print("  PyForge Report")
    print("=" * 20)

banner()
print("Everything is fine.")
banner()

ex.title: Parameters and return
ex.text:
**Parameters** are the inputs a function takes. `return` sends a result back to whoever called it.
A function that returns a value can be used inside expressions, just like `len()` or `int()`.
ex.code:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

room = area(4, 3.5)
print(room)
print(area(2, 2) + area(1, 5))

ex.why: double(3) is 6, and double(6) is 12.

ex.q: What's the difference between print() and return inside a function?
opts: return gives a value back to the caller; print only shows text on screen
print gives the value back; return shows it on screen
ex.why: A function that only prints gives back None. You can't do math with what it printed.

ex.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hi " + name)

result = greet("Mo")
print(result)
ex.why: greet prints, but returns nothing, so result is None.

ex.q: Write a function `to_fahrenheit(c)` that returns the temperature in Fahrenheit (c × 9 / 5 + 32).
ex.solution:
def to_fahrenheit(c):
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32

ex.q: Write `is_even(n)` that returns `True` if n is even and `False` otherwise.
ex.solution:
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0

ex.title: Defaults and keyword arguments
ex.text:
Give a parameter a **default** with `=`. The caller can skip it, or pass it by name.
Named (keyword) arguments make calls easier to read: `price(100, tax=0.2)`.

ex.title: Returning several values
ex.text: Return several values separated by commas. The caller can unpack them into separate variables.
ex.code:
def min_max(a, b, c):
    low = min(a, b, c)
    high = max(a, b, c)
    return low, high

lo, hi = min_max(8, 3, 11)
print(lo, hi)

ex.q: Write `split_time(seconds)` that returns hours, minutes and seconds (three values). `split_time(3725)` returns `(1, 2, 5)`.
ex.solution:
def split_time(seconds):
    h = seconds // 3600
    m = seconds % 3600 // 60
    s = seconds % 60
    return h, m, s

ex.q: Write `bmi(weight_kg, height_m)` that returns the body mass index (weight ÷ height²) rounded to 1 decimal, and `category(b)` that returns `under` below 18.5, `normal` below 25, `over` below 30, otherwise `obese`.

ex.title: Where variables live
ex.text:
Variables created inside a function are **local**: they exist only while it runs. Variables at the top level are **global** and can be read anywhere.
To **change** a global from inside a function, declare it with `global name`. Games use this a lot, since their state lives at the top level.
ex.code:
score = 0

def add_points(n):
    global score
    score += n

add_points(10)
add_points(5)
print(score)

x = 5
def change():
    x = 99
change()
print(x)
ex.why: Without `global x`, the function made a new local x. The global x is untouched.

ex.q: The counter should reach 3, but the program crashes with UnboundLocalError. Fix it.
ex.start:
clicks = 0

def click():
    clicks += 1

click()
click()
click()
print(clicks)
ex.solution:
clicks = 0

def click():
    global clicks
    clicks += 1

click()
click()
click()
print(clicks)
hints: The function needs permission to change the global variable.

ex.q: In general, which is better design?
opts: Functions that take inputs and return outputs
Functions that change lots of globals
Putting everything at the top level
ex.why: Inputs-in, outputs-out functions are easy to test and reuse. Use globals sparingly, like for game state.

ex.title: Small functions, big programs
ex.text: Good programs are built from small functions that each do one job, then combine them. Write a short **docstring** (a string right under the def) to say what a function does.

ex.q: Write `gcd(a, b)`, the greatest common divisor, using Euclid's method: while b isn't 0, replace (a, b) with (b, a % b). Then return a.
Write `is_palindrome(text)` that ignores case, spaces and punctuation: `is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")` is True. Only letters and digits count.

tests.call: is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")
is_palindrome("Was it a car or a cat I saw?")

ex.title: Test your own code with assert
ex.text: `assert condition` does nothing if the condition is True, and crashes loudly if it's False. A few asserts after a function are the simplest form of automated testing.

ex.q: Write `count_primes(n)` that returns how many primes are less than or equal to n. Write a helper `is_prime` first and use it.

challenge.q: Write `digit_sum(n)` that returns the sum of the digits of a non-negative whole number.

Write `compound(principal, rate, years, per_year=12)` that returns the balance with interest compounded per_year times a year, rounded to 2 decimals. Formula: principal × (1 + rate / per_year) ** (per_year × years). rate is a decimal, like 0.05.
challenge.start:
def compound(principal, rate, years, per_year=12):
    pass
challenge.solution:
def compound(principal, rate, years, per_year=12):
    return round(principal * (1 + rate / per_year) ** (per_year * years), 2)

challenge.q: Write `title_case(text)` that capitalizes the first letter of every word and lowercases the rest, without using .title() or .capitalize().
challenge.solution:
def title_case(text):
    out = ""
    prev = " "
    for ch in text:
        out += ch.upper() if prev == " " else ch.lower()
        prev = ch
    return out

units.title: Lists
units.blurb: Store many values in order, and process them all at once.

ex.title: Many values, one name
ex.text:
A **list** holds values in order: `[3, 1, 4]`. Index it like a string (from 0), slice it, check its `len()`.
Unlike strings, lists can be changed in place.
ex.code:
scores = [72, 88, 95, 61]
print(scores[0], scores[-1])
print(scores[1:3])
print(len(scores), sum(scores), max(scores))
scores[3] = 65
print(scores)

ex.why: b = a doesn't copy the list. Both names point to the same list. Use a.copy() or a[:] to copy.

ex.q: Which expression checks whether 7 is in the list `nums`?
Write `average(nums)` that returns the average of a list of numbers, or 0 for an empty list.

ex.title: Add, remove, sort
ex.text:
- `.append(x)` adds to the end, `.insert(i, x)` adds at position i
- `.remove(x)` deletes the first x, `.pop()` removes and returns the last item (`.pop(i)` for position i)
- `.sort()` sorts in place; `sorted(lst)` returns a new sorted list
- `.reverse()` reverses in place; `.index(x)` finds x's position
ex.code:
queue = ["Ana", "Ben"]
queue.append("Cy")
queue.insert(0, "Dee")
served = queue.pop(0)
print(served, queue)
prices = [9.5, 3, 7.25]
print(sorted(prices), prices)
prices.sort(reverse=True)
print(prices)

x = [5, 3, 8]
x.append(1)
x.sort()
print(x.pop())
ex.why: After sorting, x is [1, 3, 5, 8], and pop() removes the last item, 8.

ex.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
result = nums.sort()
print(result)
ex.why: .sort() changes the list and returns None. Use sorted(nums) if you want the result back.

ex.q: Write `remove_duplicates(items)` that returns a new list with duplicates removed, keeping the **first** time each value appears, in order.
Write `second_largest(nums)` that returns the second-largest **distinct** value, without sorting. `second_largest([4, 9, 9, 7])` is 7.
hints: Track the largest and second largest as you go through the list once.

ex.q: Write `rotate(items, k)` that returns the list rotated right by k places: `rotate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` is `[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]`. k can be bigger than the length.

ex.title: Loop, filter, transform
ex.text:
Most list work is one of three patterns:
- **map**: make a new list by transforming each item
- **filter**: keep only items that pass a test
- **reduce**: combine everything into one value (sum, max, count)
ex.code:
temps_c = [18, 25, 31, 12, 28]
temps_f = []
hot_days = []
for t in temps_c:
    temps_f.append(t * 9 / 5 + 32)
    if t > 25:
        hot_days.append(t)
print(temps_f)
print(hot_days, len(hot_days))

ex.title: List comprehensions
ex.text: A **comprehension** builds a list in one line: `[expression for item in list if condition]`. It's the Pythonic way to map and filter.
ex.code:
nums = range(1, 11)
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
words = ["hi", "hello", "hey", "yo"]
print(squares)
print(evens)
print([w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 2])
print([x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3] if x != 2])

ex.q: Write `long_words(words, n)` that returns the words longer than n characters, in lowercase. Use a comprehension.
ex.solution:
def long_words(words, n):
    return [w.lower() for w in words if len(w) > n]

ex.q: Write `running_total(nums)` that returns the running totals: `[3, 1, 4]` gives `[3, 4, 8]`.
ex.solution:
def running_total(nums):
    out = []
    total = 0
    for n in nums:
        total += n
        out.append(total)
    return out

ex.title: Positions and pairs
ex.text:
- `enumerate(lst)` gives (index, item) pairs
- `zip(a, b)` walks two lists side by side
- `text.split()` breaks text into a list of words; `" ".join(words)` glues them back
ex.code:
names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"]
scores = [91, 78, 85]
for i, name in enumerate(names, start=1):
    print(i, name)
for name, s in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name}: {s}")
words = "the quick brown fox".split()
print(words, "-".join(words))
print(" ".join(reversed("one two three".split())))

ex.q: Read a line of numbers separated by spaces (like `4 8 15 16 23 42`) and print their sum.
ex.solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]
print(sum(nums))

ex.q: Write `best_student(names, scores)` that returns the name with the highest score (two lists of the same length).
Write `chunk(items, size)` that splits a list into pieces of `size`: `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` is `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]`.
ex.solution:
def chunk(items, size):
    return [items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]

challenge.why: [[0] * 2] * 2 repeats the same inner list twice. Changing one changes both. Build grids with a comprehension instead.

challenge.q: Write `flatten(lists)` that turns a list of lists into one list. `flatten([[1, 2], [3], []])` is `[1, 2, 3]`.
challenge.solution:
def flatten(lists):
    return [x for sub in lists for x in sub]

challenge.q: Write `merge_sorted(a, b)` that merges two already-sorted lists into one sorted list without calling sort() or sorted().
Write `max_profit(prices)`: given daily stock prices, return the best profit from buying once and selling later (0 if no profit is possible).

units.title: Dictionaries & Sets
units.blurb: Look things up by name, count anything, and remove duplicates instantly.

ex.title: A dictionary maps keys to values
ex.text:
A **dictionary** stores pairs: `{"apple": 1.2, "bread": 3.5}`. Look up a value by its key with `d[key]`. Add or change with `d[key] = value`.
Keys are unique. Looking up a missing key with `d[key]` raises a KeyError; `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead.
ex.code:
prices = {"apple": 1.2, "bread": 3.5}
prices["milk"] = 2.25
prices["apple"] = 1.0
print(prices["bread"])
print(prices.get("cheese", "not sold here"))
print(len(prices), "milk" in prices)

ex.title: Looping over a dictionary
ex.text:
- `for key in d` loops over keys
- `d.values()` gives the values, `d.items()` gives (key, value) pairs
- `del d[key]` or `d.pop(key)` removes a pair

ex.q: Write `total_bill(order, menu)`. `menu` maps item names to prices, `order` maps item names to quantities. Return the total cost rounded to 2 decimals.
Write `invert(d)` that swaps keys and values: `{"a": 1, "b": 2}` becomes `{1: "a", 2: "b"}`.
ex.solution:
def invert(d):
    return {v: k for k, v in d.items()}

ex.title: The counting pattern
ex.text: To count things, use a dictionary where each key is a thing and each value is how many times you've seen it. `counts.get(x, 0) + 1` handles first sightings neatly.
ex.code:
votes = ["pizza", "tacos", "pizza", "sushi", "pizza", "tacos"]
counts = {}
for v in votes:
    counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
print(counts)
winner = max(counts, key=counts.get)
print("Winner:", winner)

ex.why: "l" appears twice, and the distinct letters are h, e, l, o.

ex.q: Write `word_counts(text)` that returns a dictionary of how often each word appears. Make it case-insensitive and ignore the punctuation `.,!?`.
Write `first_unique(text)` that returns the first character that appears only once, or None. `first_unique("swiss")` is `"w"`.

ex.title: Grouping
ex.text: Grouping is counting's cousin: each key holds a **list** of things that belong together.

ex.q: Write `group_anagrams(words)` that returns a list of groups of words that are anagrams of each other, in the order each group first appears. `["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]` gives `[["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"], ["bat"]]`.
hints: Two words are anagrams if their sorted letters are the same. Use that as the key.

ex.title: Lists of dictionaries
ex.text: Real data is often a list of records, each record a dictionary. This is exactly the shape of JSON from web APIs, so it's worth getting comfortable with.
ex.code:
movies = [
    {"title": "Inception", "year": 2010, "rating": 8.8},
    {"title": "Up", "year": 2009, "rating": 8.3},
    {"title": "Dune", "year": 2021, "rating": 8.0},
]
for m in movies:
    print(f"{m['title']} ({m['year']}): {m['rating']}")
best = max(movies, key=lambda m: m["rating"])
print("Top:", best["title"])

user = {"name": "Lee", "langs": ["Python", "SQL"], "address": {"city": "Austin"}}
print(user["langs"][-1], user["address"]["city"])

ex.q: Write `titles_after(movies, year)` that returns a sorted list of titles of movies released after the given year. Each movie is a dictionary with "title" and "year".
ex.solution:
def titles_after(movies, year):
    return sorted(m["title"] for m in movies if m["year"] > year)

ex.q: Write `average_by(records, group_key, value_key)`. It returns a dictionary mapping each group to the average of its values, rounded to 1 decimal. For example, average salary by department.

ex.title: Unique values, instant membership
ex.text:
A **set** holds unique values with no order: `{3, 1, 3}` is `{1, 3}`. Checking `x in s` is instant even for millions of items.
Set math: `a | b` union, `a & b` intersection, `a - b` difference.

ex.code: print(sorted({5, 1, 5, 3, 1}))

ex.q: Write `two_sum(nums, target)` that returns the indexes `(i, j)` (i < j) of two numbers that add up to target, or None. Do it in one pass using a dictionary of values you've already seen.
hints: For each n, check whether target − n was already seen.

ex.q: Write `is_pangram(text)` that returns True if the text uses every letter a–z at least once.
ex.solution:
def is_pangram(text):
    return set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz") <= set(text.lower())

tests.call: is_pangram("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")

challenge.why: 1 and 1.0 are equal and hash the same, so they're the same key. The key keeps its first form, 1.
^ is symmetric difference, items in exactly one of the sets.

challenge.q: Write `most_common(items)` that returns the item that appears most often (if there's a tie, the one that appears first).
Write `common_friends(a, b)` where a and b are lists of names. Return the names in both lists, sorted alphabetically, with no duplicates.
challenge.solution:
def common_friends(a, b):
    return sorted(set(a) & set(b))

challenge.q: Write `roman_to_int(s)` that converts a Roman numeral to an integer. (I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. A smaller value before a larger one is subtracted, like IV = 4.)

units.title: Grids
units.blurb: Lists of lists. Game boards, spreadsheets, images and maps all live here.

ex.title: A list of lists
ex.text:
A grid is a list of rows, and each row is a list. `grid[r][c]` is row r, column c.
Create grids with a comprehension so each row is its own list: `[[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]`.
ex.code:
grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9],
]
print(grid[1][2])
for row in grid:
    print(" ".join(str(x) for x in row))
empty = [["." for _ in range(4)] for _ in range(2)]
empty[0][3] = "#"
print(empty)

ex.q: Write `row_sums(grid)` and `col_sums(grid)` that return lists of the sums of each row and each column.
Write `diagonals(grid)` for a square grid. Return a pair: the sum of the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) and the sum of the other diagonal.
ex.solution:
def diagonals(grid):
    n = len(grid)
    main = sum(grid[i][i] for i in range(n))
    anti = sum(grid[i][n - 1 - i] for i in range(n))
    return main, anti

ex.q: A magic square has every row, every column and both diagonals adding up to the same number. Write `is_magic(grid)`.
ex.solution:
def is_magic(grid):
    n = len(grid)
    target = sum(grid[0])
    sums = [sum(row) for row in grid]
    sums += [sum(grid[r][c] for r in range(n)) for c in range(n)]
    sums.append(sum(grid[i][i] for i in range(n)))
    sums.append(sum(grid[i][n - 1 - i] for i in range(n)))
    return all(s == target for s in sums)

ex.title: Looking around a cell
ex.text: Many grid problems ask "what's around this cell?" Loop over the 8 directions with `dr` and `dc` from −1 to 1, skip (0, 0), and check you're still inside the grid.

ex.q: Write `minesweeper_numbers(board)`. The board is a list of strings with `*` for mines and `.` for empty. Return a list of strings where each `.` is replaced by the number of neighbouring mines (mines stay `*`).

ex.title: Conway's Game of Life
ex.text:
Each cell is alive or dead. Every generation, all at once:
- a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive
- a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours comes alive
- every other cell dies or stays dead
The key detail: build a **new** grid, so changes don't affect neighbours you haven't processed yet.

ex.q: Write `life_step(grid)`. The grid is a list of lists of 0 and 1. Return the next generation as a new grid (cells outside the edges count as dead).

tests.label: A blinker flips from vertical to horizontal

ex.title: Transpose and rotate
ex.text:
**Transposing** swaps rows and columns: row r becomes column r. `zip(*grid)` does it in one move.
Rotating 90° clockwise is "transpose, then reverse each row".
ex.code:
g = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
t = [list(col) for col in zip(*g)]
print(t)
rotated = [list(reversed(col)) for col in zip(*g)]
print(rotated)

ex.q: Write `rotate_cw(grid)` that returns the grid rotated 90° clockwise, without using zip.
Write `spiral(grid)` that returns all values in clockwise spiral order, starting top-left. `[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]` gives `[1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 8, 7, 4, 5]`.
hints: Keep four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and shrink them after each lap.

ex.title: Searching in 8 directions
ex.text: To find a word in a letter grid, try every starting cell and every direction `(dr, dc)`. Walk step by step and compare letters until the word matches or you fall off the grid.

ex.q: Write `find_word(grid, word)`. The grid is a list of equal-length strings. Return `(row, col, direction)` for the first match scanning rows top to bottom and columns left to right, trying directions in this order: right, down, down-right, up-right, left, up, up-left, down-left. Directions are named `"right"`, `"down"` and so on (e.g. `"down-right"`). Return None if it's not there.

Write `flood_count(grid, r, c)`. The grid is a list of strings of `.` (open) and `#` (wall). Return how many open cells you can reach from (r, c) moving up, down, left and right. Use a list as a to-do stack and a set of visited cells.

challenge.code:
g = [[r * 3 + c for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)]
print(g[2][1], sum(g[1]))

challenge.q: Write `transpose(grid)` without zip.
challenge.solution:
def transpose(grid):
    return [[grid[r][c] for r in range(len(grid))] for c in range(len(grid[0]))]

challenge.q: Write `tic_winner(board)`. The board is 3 strings of `X`, `O` or `.`. Return `"X"` or `"O"` if someone has three in a row (row, column or diagonal), otherwise None.
Write `island_count(grid)`: count groups of connected `#` cells (up/down/left/right) in a list of strings.

units.title: Searching & Sorting
units.blurb: The algorithms every programmer knows by heart, and how to tell fast code from slow code.

ex.title: Linear search
ex.text: To find something in an unsorted list, you check items one by one. In the worst case you look at all n items. That's called **linear** time, written **O(n)**.

ex.title: Binary search
ex.text:
If the list is **sorted**, you can do much better. Look at the middle: if the target is bigger, throw away the left half; if smaller, the right half. Each step halves the search.
A million items takes about 20 steps. That's **O(log n)**.

ex.q: Binary search needs at most about how many steps for a sorted list of 1,000,000 items?
ex.why: 2 to the 20th is about a million, so 20 halvings get you down to one item.

ex.q: Write `binary_search(items, target)` that returns the index of target in the sorted list, or -1. Don't use `.index()` or `in`.
Write `first_at_least(items, x)` for a sorted list: return the index of the first item that is ≥ x, or `len(items)` if there's none. It's a binary search that keeps going after a match.

ex.title: Bubble sort
ex.text:
Walk through the list comparing neighbours, swapping any that are out of order. The biggest value "bubbles" to the end. Repeat until a full pass makes no swaps.
It's simple and slow: about n² comparisons, **O(n²)**.

ex.why: That's one bubble pass. 3 moves past 1, then past 2.

ex.q: Selection sort: find the smallest item in the unsorted part and swap it to the front, then repeat for the rest. Write `selection_sort(a)` that returns a new sorted list without using sort() or sorted().
Insertion sort: take each item and slide it left until it's in the right place among the items before it (like sorting cards in your hand). Write `insertion_sort(a)`.
Insertion sort is fast on which kind of input?
opts: Lists that are already almost sorted
ex.why: Each item only slides a short way, so it's close to O(n).

ex.title: key functions
ex.text:
In real code you use Python's built-in `sorted()` (it's a highly tuned merge/insertion hybrid called Timsort). The skill is choosing **what to sort by**.
`key=` takes a function that turns each item into the value to compare. `lambda x: ...` writes a tiny function inline.
ex.code:
words = ["banana", "Kiwi", "apple", "Cherry"]
print(sorted(words))
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))
print(sorted(words, key=len))
people = [("Ana", 31), ("Ben", 25), ("Cy", 31)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True))
print(sorted(["bb", "a", "ccc", "dd"], key=len))
ex.why: Sorting by length. Python's sort is stable, so equal-length "bb" and "dd" keep their original order.

ex.q: Write `leaderboard(scores)`. `scores` is a list of `(name, points)` pairs. Return the names sorted by points, highest first, and alphabetically when points tie.
ex.solution:
def leaderboard(scores):
    return [name for name, pts in sorted(scores, key=lambda s: (-s[1], s[0]))]
hints: Sort by a tuple: key=lambda s: (-s[1], s[0]).

ex.q: Write `sort_files(names)` that sorts file names the way humans expect: by the number inside them. `["img12.png", "img2.png", "img1.png"]` becomes `["img1.png", "img2.png", "img12.png"]`. Each name has exactly one number in it.

ex.title: Big-O in plain English
ex.text:
Big-O describes how work grows as the input grows:
- **O(1)**: same work no matter the size (dict lookup, `x in set`)
- **O(log n)**: halves each step (binary search)
- **O(n)**: one pass (linear search, sum)
- **O(n log n)**: good sorting
- **O(n²)**: a loop inside a loop over the same data
For 1,000,000 items, O(n²) is a trillion steps. O(n log n) is about 20 million.

ex.q: What's the Big-O of checking `x in my_list` versus `x in my_set`?
opts: O(n) for the list, O(1) for the set
ex.why: A list is checked item by item. A set uses hashing to jump straight to the answer.

ex.q: `has_duplicates_slow` compares every pair, O(n²). Write `has_duplicates(items)` that does the same job in O(n) using a set.

challenge.q: Which algorithm needs the list to be sorted first?
opts: Counting how many items there are

challenge.code: print(sorted([3, -7, 2, -1], key=abs))

challenge.q: Write `bubble_count(a)` that returns how many swaps bubble sort makes to sort the list.
Write `kth_smallest(a, k)` (k starts at 1) without sorting the whole list: do k rounds of selection sort and return the item in position k − 1.

units.title: Recursion
units.blurb: Functions that call themselves. Elegant solutions to problems that branch, nest and explore.

ex.title: A function that calls itself
ex.text:
A **recursive** function solves a problem by solving a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs:
- a **base case** that answers directly, with no further calls
- a **recursive case** that calls itself on something smaller
Without a base case, it calls itself forever and Python stops it with a RecursionError.
ex.code:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Liftoff!")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)

countdown(3)

ex.title: Factorial, the classic
ex.text:
5! = 5 × 4!, and 4! = 4 × 3!, and so on down to 1! = 1. That definition **is** the code.
Each call waits on the call stack until the one below it returns.

ex.why: The print happens after the recursive call returns, so the deepest call prints first.

ex.q: Write `sum_list(nums)` recursively. The sum of an empty list is 0; otherwise it's the first item plus the sum of the rest. No loops and no sum().
Write `power(base, exp)` recursively for whole numbers exp ≥ 0, without using `**` or pow().

ex.title: The Fibonacci trap
ex.text:
`fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` is beautiful and **terribly slow**: fib(40) makes over 300 million calls, because it solves the same small problems again and again.
**Memoization** fixes it: remember answers in a dictionary and reuse them.

ex.q: Write a memoized `fib(n)` that returns the nth Fibonacci number (fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1) fast enough to compute fib(200).
Climbing stairs: you can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. Write `ways(n)` that returns how many different ways there are to climb n steps. Use recursion with memoization (ways(0) = 1).
hints: The last move was either 1 step or 2 steps, so ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2).

ex.q: Write `is_pal(s)` recursively. A string is a palindrome if its first and last characters match and the middle is a palindrome. Empty and 1-character strings are palindromes.

ex.title: Nested data
ex.text:
Recursion shines on data that contains smaller copies of itself: folders inside folders, comments with replies, JSON inside JSON.
`isinstance(x, list)` checks if something is a list.

ex.q: Write `flatten(items)` that turns any nesting of lists into one flat list. `flatten([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`.
Write `depth(items)`: how deeply a list is nested. A list with no lists inside has depth 1; `[1, [2, [3]]]` has depth 3.

ex.title: Merge sort
ex.text: Merge sort is recursion's star: split the list in half, sort each half (recursively), then merge the two sorted halves. It's **O(n log n)**, fast even on millions of items.

ex.q: Write `merge_sort(items)` yourself, including a `merge` helper. No sort() or sorted().

ex.title: Permutations and subsets
ex.text: Recursion is the natural way to generate **all** possibilities. The permutations of `abc` are: `a` + every permutation of `bc`, then `b` + every permutation of `ac`, then `c` + every permutation of `ab`.

ex.q: Write `subsets(items)` that returns every subset of a list, as lists. The subsets of `[]` are `[[]]`. For the rest, take the subsets without the first item, plus each of those with the first item added at the front. Order: without-first ones first.

Write `fill(grid, r, c, new)` that does a flood fill, like a paint bucket. `grid` is a list of lists of characters. Change the cell at (r, c) and every connected cell (up/down/left/right) that has the same original character to `new`. Do it recursively and return the grid.
ex.start:
def fill(grid, r, c, new):
    pass

tests.call: ["".join(row) for row in fill([list("..#."), list(".##."), list("...#")], 0, 0, "o")]

ex.q: Why does a RecursionError happen?
opts: The function keeps calling itself without reaching a base case (or nests too deeply)
A loop is inside the function

challenge.why: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, that's 4 halvings plus the base case 1.

challenge.q: Write `reverse(s)` recursively without slicing with a step or reversed().
Write `binary_search(items, target, lo=0, hi=None)` recursively. Return the index or -1.
challenge.start:
def binary_search(items, target, lo=0, hi=None):
    pass

challenge.q: Write `make_change(amount, coins)` that returns the number of ways to make `amount` from unlimited coins of the given values. `make_change(4, [1, 2])` is 3 (1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 2+2).
hints: Either use the first coin (and keep all coins available), or never use it again.

units.title: Files & Data
units.blurb: Read and write real files. Text, CSV spreadsheets and JSON, the formats the world runs on.

ex.title: open() and with
ex.text:
`open(path)` opens a file. Use it in a `with` block so the file is closed automatically, even if something goes wrong.
- `f.read()` gives the whole file as one string
- `for line in f:` reads line by line (each line ends with `\n`, so use `.strip()`)
In this app, each lesson has its own little folder of files. Look under **Files in your folder** after running.

files.notes.txt:
Buy oat milk
Finish Unit 11
Call the landlord

ex.title: Writing files
ex.text: Open with mode `"w"` to write (it **replaces** the file) or `"a"` to append to the end. `f.write(text)` doesn't add a newline for you.
ex.code:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("started\n")
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("still going\n")
print(open("log.txt").read())

ex.q: You open an existing file with mode "w" and write one line. What happens to what was in it before?
opts: The new line is added at the end
ex.why: Mode "w" starts the file fresh. Use "a" to add to the end.

ex.q: `todo.txt` has one task per line, some starting with `[x]` (done). Write `count_open(path)` that returns how many tasks are not done. Ignore blank lines.

files.todo.txt:
[x] Email Sam
Book dentist
[x] Pay rent

Renew passport

ex.q: Write `save_lines(path, items)` that writes each item on its own line, and `load_lines(path)` that reads them back as a list of strings (without newlines).

tests.exec:
save_lines("shopping.txt", ["eggs", "rice", "limes"])
assert load_lines("shopping.txt") == ["eggs", "rice", "limes"], "Reading back should give the same list"
assert open("shopping.txt").read() == "eggs\nrice\nlimes\n", "Each item goes on its own line"
tests.label: Saving and loading round-trips

ex.title: Spreadsheets as text
ex.text:
**CSV** (comma-separated values) is how spreadsheets travel. Each line is a row; commas separate the columns; the first row is usually headers.
The `csv` module handles the tricky parts (like commas inside quotes). `csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the headers.
ex.code:
import csv
with open("sales.csv") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["region"], float(row["amount"]))

import csv, io
text = 'name,city\n"Lee, Ana",Oslo\n'
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)))
print(len(rows[1]))
ex.why: The quotes keep "Lee, Ana" together as one value, even though it contains a comma.

ex.q: Write `totals_by_region(path)` that reads a sales CSV (columns date, region, amount) and returns a dictionary of total amount per region, each rounded to 2 decimals.
Write `write_report(path, totals)` that writes a CSV with headers `region,total` and one row per region, sorted by total (highest first). Use `csv.writer`.
ex.solution:
import csv

def write_report(path, totals):
    with open(path, "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["region", "total"])
        for region, total in sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
            w.writerow([region, total])

tests.exec:
write_report("report.csv", {"North": 360.5, "East": 15.25, "South": 100.0})
lines = open("report.csv").read().splitlines()
assert lines == ["region,total", "North,360.5", "South,100.0", "East,15.25"], f"report.csv contains: {lines}"
tests.label: The report is sorted with a header row

ex.title: Data with structure
ex.text:
**JSON** stores nested data (dicts, lists, strings, numbers, true/false, null) as text. It's what web APIs send and what many apps use for settings.
- `json.load(f)` / `json.dump(data, f)` read and write files
- `json.loads(text)` / `json.dumps(data)` work with strings
`indent=2` makes it readable.
ex.code:
import json
settings = {"theme": "dark", "volume": 0.8, "shortcuts": ["ctrl+s", "ctrl+z"], "beta": False}
with open("settings.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(settings, f, indent=2)
print(open("settings.json").read())
loaded = json.load(open("settings.json"))
print(loaded["shortcuts"][0], loaded["beta"])

import json
print(json.dumps({"ok": True, "n": None}))
ex.why: JSON spells them true, false and null, and always uses double quotes.

ex.q: `orders.json` holds a list of orders, each with "customer" and "items" (a list of {"name", "price", "qty"}). Write `biggest_spender(path)` that returns the customer who spent the most in total.
Write `csv_to_json(csv_path, json_path)` that converts a CSV file into a JSON list of objects (one per row, keys from the header). Numbers can stay as strings. Return the number of rows written.
ex.solution:
import csv, json

def csv_to_json(csv_path, json_path):
    with open(csv_path) as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    with open(json_path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(rows, f, indent=2)
    return len(rows)

tests.exec:
import json
n = csv_to_json("people.csv", "people.json")
assert n == 2, "Return the number of rows"
assert json.load(open("people.json")) == [{"name": "Ada", "role": "engineer"}, {"name": "Linus", "role": "maintainer"}], "people.json should hold one object per row"
tests.label: CSV becomes a JSON list of objects

ex.title: Working with folders
ex.text:
The `os` module talks to the file system:
- `os.listdir(folder)` lists names in a folder
- `os.path.join(a, b)` builds paths safely
- `os.path.splitext(name)` splits `photo.jpg` into `("photo", ".jpg")`
- `os.path.exists(p)`, `os.path.getsize(p)`, `os.makedirs(p, exist_ok=True)`
`os.walk(folder)` visits every folder inside, recursively.
ex.code:
import os
for name in sorted(os.listdir("inbox")):
    base, ext = os.path.splitext(name)
    size = os.path.getsize(os.path.join("inbox", name))
    print(f"{base:<12} {ext:<6} {size} bytes")

ex.q: Write `count_by_type(folder)` that returns a dictionary counting files by extension (lowercase, without the dot) in a folder **and all its subfolders**. Files without an extension count under `"none"`.
Write `backup(src, dest)` that copies every `.txt` file from the `src` folder into the `dest` folder (create it if needed), adding `.bak` to each name. Return the sorted list of new file names.

challenge.q: Why use `with open(...) as f:` instead of `f = open(...)`?
opts: It closes the file automatically, even if an error happens
It's the only way to write files
It reads the file into memory

challenge.code:
with open("t.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("a")
    f.write("b\n")
with open("t.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("c")
print(open("t.txt").read().split("\n"))

challenge.q: Write `longest_line(path)` that returns the longest line in a text file (without the newline). If several tie, return the first.

files.poem.txt:
Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,
And sorry I could not travel both
And be one traveler, long I stood

tests.expect: 'Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,'

challenge.q: Write `merge_json(a_path, b_path, out_path)`: both files hold a JSON object. Write a merged object to out_path where keys from b override keys from a, and return the merged dictionary.
challenge.solution:
import json

def merge_json(a_path, b_path, out_path):
    merged = json.load(open(a_path))
    merged.update(json.load(open(b_path)))
    with open(out_path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(merged, f)
    return merged

units.title: Errors, Debugging & Testing
units.blurb: Read error messages like a pro, handle the unexpected, and prove your code works.

ex.title: Errors are messages, not failures
ex.text:
When Python crashes it prints a **traceback**. Read it from the **bottom up**:
- the last line names the error type and what went wrong
- the lines above show where: file, line number, and the code on that line
- the chain of calls shows how the program got there
Most bugs are found in under a minute by reading that last line carefully.

ex.q: Which error do you get from `int("12a")`?
ex.why: The type is right (a string), but its content can't become an int.

ex.q: Which error do you get from `"total: " + 5`?
Which error do you get from `{"a": 1}["b"]`?
Which error do you get from `[1, 2, 3].push(4)`?
ex.why: Lists don't have a push method (it's append), so the attribute doesn't exist.

ex.q: This should print the last item of each list, but it crashes. Read the error, then fix it.

ex.title: try and except
ex.text:
Wrap risky code in `try`. If a matching error happens, Python jumps to `except` instead of crashing.
- catch **specific** errors (`except ValueError:`), never everything blindly
- `else:` runs if no error happened; `finally:` always runs
Use it at the edges of your program: user input, files, networks.

ex.code:
try:
    x = 10 / 0
    print("A")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("B")
finally:
    print("C")

ex.q: Write `safe_float(text, default=0.0)` that converts text to a float, or returns the default if it can't.
Keep asking for an age until the user types a whole number from 0 to 120. For bad input print `Please enter a number from 0 to 120`. Then print `Age saved: N`.

tests.stdout:
twenty
Please enter a number from 0 to 120
-5
Please enter a number from 0 to 120
31
Age saved: 31

ex.q: Write `read_config(path)` that returns the JSON in the file as a dictionary. If the file doesn't exist return `{}`. If it isn't valid JSON, also return `{}`.

ex.title: raise
ex.text:
When a function gets input it can't handle, **raise** an error with a clear message instead of returning something wrong. The caller decides what to do.
You can make your own error types by subclassing `Exception`.

ex.q: Write `withdraw(balance, amount)` that returns the new balance. Raise `ValueError("amount must be positive")` if amount ≤ 0, and `ValueError("insufficient funds")` if amount is more than the balance.

tests.label: Bad amounts raise clear errors

ex.q: Write `parse_time(text)` that turns `"HH:MM"` into minutes after midnight. Raise `ValueError` for anything malformed or out of range (hours 0–23, minutes 0–59).

tests.label: Malformed times raise ValueError

ex.title: A debugging routine that works
ex.text:
1. **Reproduce** it with the smallest input that fails.
2. **Read** the error, or compare the actual output to what you expected.
3. **Inspect**: print the values right before the failure.
4. **Hypothesize** one cause, change one thing, rerun.
5. Once fixed, **add a test** so it never comes back.
Most bugs are off-by-one, wrong types, or a case you didn't think of (empty input, zero, negatives, duplicates).

ex.title: Watch your code run
ex.text:
Professional editors have a **debugger**: it pauses your program and lets you run it one line at a time while watching every variable. PyForge has one too. Press **Step through** below, then use ▶ to move forward and ◀ to go back.
- the highlighted line is the one **about to run**
- variables that just changed light up
- when a function is called, you see its own variables, and the call stack shows who called whom

This program has a bug: the average of 90, 80 and 70 should be 80, but it prints about 35.6. Step through it and watch `total` change.
ex.code:
def average(scores):
    total = 0
    for s in scores:
        total = total + s
        total = total / len(scores)
    return total

print(average([90, 80, 70]))

ex.q: `largest(nums)` works for most lists but gives the wrong answer for one test. Use **Step** to watch `best` and find out why, then fix it (don't use `max()`).
`count_in_range(nums, lo, hi)` should count numbers from lo to hi **inclusive**. One test fails. Find and fix the bug.
ex.start:
def count_in_range(nums, lo, hi):
    return len([n for n in nums if lo < n <= hi])
ex.solution:
def count_in_range(nums, lo, hi):
    return len([n for n in nums if lo <= n <= hi])

ex.q: `add_tag` is supposed to return a list with just one new tag each time it's called without a list, but tags pile up between calls. Fix it (this is Python's famous mutable-default trap).

tests.exec:
a = add_tag("python")
b = add_tag("games")
assert b == ["games"], f"A fresh call should return ['games'], got {b}"
assert add_tag("x", ["y"]) == ["y", "x"], "Passing a list still works"
tests.label: Each call gets its own list

ex.q: The average should be 2.5 for [1, 2, 3, 4], but it comes out wrong. Fix it.

Write your own tests! Below is `is_valid_username`. Write a function `test_usernames()` that uses `assert` to check at least these cases: a normal name passes, an empty name fails, a name with a space fails, a name over 15 characters fails, and one starting with a digit fails.

tests.exec: test_usernames()
tests.label: Your tests pass on the correct function

tests.exec:
real = is_valid_username
broken = [lambda n: len(n) <= 15 and (n[:1].isalpha() if n else True) and " " not in n,
          lambda n: 0 < len(n) and n[0].isalpha() and " " not in n,
          lambda n: 0 < len(n) <= 15 and " " not in n,
          lambda n: 0 < len(n) <= 15 and n[0].isalpha()]
globals_ = test_usernames.__globals__
caught = 0
for b in broken:
    globals_["is_valid_username"] = b
    try:
        test_usernames()
    except AssertionError:
        caught += 1
globals_["is_valid_username"] = real
assert caught == len(broken), f"Your tests caught {caught} of {len(broken)} broken versions. Cover all five cases."
tests.label: Your tests catch broken versions

challenge.why: finally runs before the function actually returns.

challenge.q: What's wrong with `except:` on its own (no error type)?
opts: It hides every error, including bugs and Ctrl-C, so problems go silent

challenge.q: Write `divide_all(nums, d)` that returns a list of n / d for each n. If d is 0, raise `ZeroDivisionError("can't divide by zero")` before doing anything.

tests.label: Dividing by zero raises a clear error

challenge.q: This should collect the even numbers, but it skips some. Fix it without changing what the function returns.
challenge.solution:
def evens(nums):
    return [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]

units.title: Classes & Objects
units.blurb: Model the real world in code. Bundle data with the behavior that belongs to it.

ex.title: Blueprints and objects
ex.text: A **class** is a blueprint; each **object** made from it has its own data. `__init__` runs when you create one and sets up its **attributes**. Methods are functions that belong to the class; their first parameter, `self`, is the object itself.
ex.code:
class Pet:
    def __init__(self, name, kind):
        self.name = name
        self.kind = kind
        self.hunger = 5

    def feed(self, amount=2):
        self.hunger = max(0, self.hunger - amount)

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.name} the {self.kind} (hunger {self.hunger})"

rex = Pet("Rex", "dog")
tom = Pet("Tom", "cat")
rex.feed()
print(rex.describe())
print(tom.describe())

ex.why: tick returns self, so the calls chain on the same object.

ex.q: What does `self` refer to inside a method?
opts: The object the method was called on

ex.q: Write a class `Rectangle` with attributes `width` and `height`, and methods `area()`, `perimeter()` and `is_square()`.

Write a class `Thermostat` with `target` (starts at 20) and methods `up()` and `down()` that change it by 0.5, never going below 10 or above 30, and `status(current)` that returns `"heating"` if current is below target, `"cooling"` if above, else `"idle"`.

tests.exec:
t = Thermostat()
t.up(); t.up()
assert t.target == 21, f"Two ups from 20 should give 21, got {t.target}"
for _ in range(100):
    t.up()
assert t.target == 30, "The target can't go over 30"
assert t.status(25) == "heating" and t.status(30) == "idle" and t.status(31) == "cooling"
tests.label: Target limits and status work

ex.title: Special methods
ex.text:
Methods with double underscores let your objects work with Python's built-in syntax:
- `__str__` controls `print(obj)`, `__repr__` how it shows up in lists and the console
- `__eq__` defines `==`, `__lt__` defines `<` (which also makes `sorted()` work)
- `__add__` defines `+`, `__len__` defines `len()`

ex.q: Write a `Vector` class for 2D vectors with `x` and `y`. Support `v + w`, `v * number` (scaling), `==`, `length()` (using math.hypot), and a repr like `Vector(3, 4)`.

ex.title: Class attributes
ex.text: Attributes set on the class itself (not on `self`) are shared by all objects. Good for constants and counters across all instances.
ex.code:
class Ticket:
    next_id = 1
    PRICE = 12.5

    def __init__(self, seat):
        self.id = Ticket.next_id
        Ticket.next_id += 1
        self.seat = seat

a, b = Ticket("A1"), Ticket("A2")
print(a.id, b.id, b.PRICE)

ex.title: Inheritance
ex.text:
A **subclass** gets everything from its parent and can add or **override** methods. `super().__init__(...)` runs the parent's setup.
Use inheritance for "is a" relationships: a Square **is a** Shape.

ex.q: Write a base class `Shape` with an `area()` that returns 0 and a `describe()` that returns `"<ClassName> with area <area rounded to 2>"` (use `type(self).__name__`). Then write `Circle(r)` and `Square(side)` that override `area()`.

ex.title: Composition
ex.text: Often an object should **have** other objects rather than **be** one. A Playlist has Songs; a Car has an Engine. Composition is usually simpler and more flexible than deep inheritance.

ex.q: Write a `Cart` that has items. `add(name, price, qty=1)` adds an item (adding to the quantity if it's already there), `remove(name)` deletes it, `total()` returns the total rounded to 2, and `len(cart)` gives the number of distinct items.

tests.exec:
c = Cart()
c.add("pen", 1.5, 2)
c.add("pad", 4)
c.add("pen", 1.5)
assert c.total() == 8.5, f"total should be 8.5, got {c.total()}"
assert len(c) == 2, "len(cart) counts distinct items"
c.remove("pad")
assert c.total() == 4.5
tests.label: Adding, removing and totals

ex.title: @dataclass
ex.text: For classes that mostly hold data, `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you from type-annotated fields. Add `order=True` to make them sortable.
ex.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(order=True)
class Task:
    priority: int
    title: 'str'
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

tasks = [Task(2, "Email"), Task(1, "Fix bug", ["urgent"]), Task(3, "Lunch")]
print(sorted(tasks)[0])
print(Task(1, "a") == Task(1, "a"))

ex.q: Write a dataclass `Book` with `title` (str), `author` (str), `pages` (int) and `read` (bool, default False). Then write `unread_pages(books)` that returns the total pages of unread books.

ex.title: Properties
ex.text: `@property` makes a method look like an attribute, so you can compute a value or protect one with validation without changing how callers use it.

ex.q: Write a class `Account` with an `owner` and a read-only `balance` property (starts at 0, stored in `self._balance`). Add `deposit(amount)` (raises ValueError for amounts ≤ 0). Trying to set `account.balance = ...` directly should fail with an AttributeError.

tests.label: balance is read-only and deposits are validated

challenge.q: Write a `Stack` class with `push(x)`, `pop()` (raise IndexError("empty stack") when empty), `peek()`, `is_empty()` and `len()` support.

tests.label: The stack works and guards against empty pops

challenge.q: Write a dataclass `Point` with x and y, and `order=True`. Then `closest(points, target)` returns the point nearest to target (by straight-line distance).
challenge.start:
from dataclasses import dataclass
import math

units.title: Intermediate Python
units.blurb: The features that separate "I can write Python" from "I can read anyone's Python": closures, flexible arguments, references, generators, decorators and context managers.

ex.title: Pass functions around
ex.text: In Python a function is a value, like a number or a list. You can store it in a variable, put it in a dictionary, or pass it to another function. You've already done this with `sorted(words, key=len)`: `len` is passed in, not called.

ex.title: Scope and closures
ex.text:
Python looks names up in order: **L**ocal (inside this function), **E**nclosing (an outer function), **G**lobal (the file), **B**uilt-in. That's the LEGB rule.
A function defined inside another one remembers the outer variables even after the outer function has finished. That's a **closure**. To *change* an outer variable, declare it `nonlocal`.
Press **Step through** to watch `count` live on inside the closure.
ex.code:
def make_counter():
    count = 0

    def tick():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count

    return tick

clicks = make_counter()
clicks()
clicks()
print(clicks())

other = make_counter()
print(other())

ex.why: inner() finds x in the enclosing function first. The assignment inside outer() created a new local x and didn't touch the global one.

ex.q: Write `make_multiplier(factor)` that returns a function. The returned function multiplies its argument by `factor`. Then `double = make_multiplier(2)` and `double(21)` gives `42`.
Write `make_bank(balance)` that returns two functions, `deposit(amount)` and `get_balance()`, sharing one balance through a closure (no classes, no globals). `deposit` returns the new balance.

tests.exec:
deposit, get_balance = make_bank(100)
assert deposit(50) == 150 and deposit(25) == 175, "deposit returns the new balance"
assert get_balance() == 175, "both functions share the same balance"
d2, g2 = make_bank(0)
d2(5)
assert g2() == 5 and get_balance() == 175, "each bank has its own balance"
tests.label: Two functions, one shared balance

ex.title: *args and **kwargs
ex.text:
- `*args` collects any number of extra positional arguments into a **tuple**
- `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a **dict**
- anything after a bare `*` must be passed by keyword: `def save(path, *, overwrite=False)`
- the same stars **unpack** when calling: `f(*my_list, **my_dict)`

This is how `print()` accepts any number of values, and how libraries pass options through.

ex.q: Write `average(*nums)` that returns the average of any number of arguments, rounded to 2 decimals, or `None` if there are none.

Write `tag(name, *children, **attrs)` that builds an HTML string. Attributes appear in the order given, and `class_` becomes `class` (since `class` is a Python keyword). `tag("a", "Docs", href="/docs", class_="link")` gives `Docs`. `tag("br")` gives `

`, and children are joined with no spaces.
Write `connect(host, *, port=443, timeout=10)` where `port` and `timeout` are **keyword-only** (calling `connect("x", 80)` must raise `TypeError`). Return the string `"host:port (timeout s)"`.
ex.start:
def connect(host, port=443, timeout=10):
    return f"{host}:{port} ({timeout}s)"
ex.solution:
def connect(host, *, port=443, timeout=10):
    return f"{host}:{port} ({timeout}s)"

tests.label: Port can only be given by name

ex.title: Variables are labels
ex.text:
A variable isn't a box holding a value. It's a **label stuck on an object**. `b = a` sticks a second label on the *same* list, so changing it through `b` changes what `a` sees too. This one idea explains a huge number of real bugs.
- `==` asks "equal values?", `is` asks "the very same object?"
- `a[:]`, `list(a)` or `a.copy()` make a **shallow** copy (a new outer list, same inner items)
- `copy.deepcopy(a)` copies everything, all the way down
Step through this one and watch which names change.
ex.code:
import copy

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a, a is b)

c = a.copy()
c.append(5)
print(a, c, a == c)

grid = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
shallow = grid.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(grid)
shallow[0][0] = 9
print(grid, deep)

row = [0] * 3
board = [row] * 2
board[0][1] = "X"
print(board)
ex.why: `[row] * 2` puts the same list in the board twice. Build grids with `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]` so each row is its own list.

ex.code:
def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

add_item("apple")
print(add_item("pear"))
ex.why: The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and reused by every call. Use `basket=None` and create a new list inside.

ex.q: `add_tag(tags, new)` should return a new list with the tag added, **without changing** the list it was given. It currently changes the caller's list. Fix it.
ex.solution:
def add_tag(tags, new):
    return tags + [new]

tests.exec:
mine = ["python"]
result = add_tag(mine, "sql")
assert result == ["python", "sql"], f"Expected ['python', 'sql'], got {result}"
assert mine == ["python"], "The original list must not change"
tests.label: Returns a new list and leaves the original alone

ex.q: `log_event` should start a fresh list each time it's called without a `log`. Right now events from different calls pile up. Fix the classic default-argument bug.

tests.exec:
assert log_event("start") == ["start"]
assert log_event("stop") == ["stop"], "Each call without a log should start fresh"
shared = []
log_event("a", shared); log_event("b", shared)
assert shared == ["a", "b"], "Passing your own list still works"
tests.label: No events leak between calls

ex.title: What a for loop really does
ex.text:
`for x in thing` calls `iter(thing)` to get an **iterator**, then calls `next()` on it until it raises `StopIteration`. Anything that follows this protocol works in a for loop: lists, strings, files, dictionaries.
A **generator** is the easy way to make your own. Use `yield` instead of `return`: the function pauses at each `yield`, hands back a value, and continues from the same spot next time. Values are made **one at a time, only when needed**, so a generator can even be infinite.

ex.code:
squares = (n * n for n in range(4))
print(sum(squares))
print(sum(squares))
ex.why: A generator can only be used once. The first sum() consumed it, so the second one sees nothing.

ex.q: Write a generator `fib()` that yields the Fibonacci numbers forever: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, … Then `first(n, gen)` returns the first n values as a list (use `itertools.islice` or `next()` in a loop).

tests.call: next(x for x in fib() if x > 1_000_000)
tests.label: Infinite, but only computes what's needed

ex.q:
Generators chain into memory-friendly **pipelines**, like a factory line. Write three generators:
- `read_lines(text)` yields each line of `text` with whitespace stripped, skipping blank lines
- `parse(lines)` turns lines like `"coffee,4.50"` into tuples `("coffee", 4.5)`
- `over(items, limit)` yields only items whose price is more than `limit`
Then `list(over(parse(read_lines(DATA)), 5))` gives the expensive purchases.
ex.start:
DATA = """
coffee,4.50
headphones,59.99

book,12.00
gum,1.25
"""

def read_lines(text):
    pass

def parse(lines):
    pass

def over(items, limit):
    pass

tests.label: Each stage is a generator (uses yield)

ex.q: Why use a generator to process a 50 GB log file instead of reading it into a list?
opts: It handles one line at a time, so memory stays tiny
Lists can't hold strings that long

ex.title: Wrapping functions
ex.text:
A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a new, upgraded one. `@timer` above a `def` is shorthand for `slow_task = timer(slow_task)`. Frameworks use them everywhere: `@app.route("/home")` in Flask, `@pytest.fixture`, `@lru_cache`.
`functools.wraps` copies the original function's name and docstring onto the wrapper, so tools and error messages still show the right name.

ex.why: Decorators apply bottom-up. dashes wraps word first, then stars wraps the result.

ex.q: Write a decorator `count_calls` that counts how many times the decorated function is called. Store the count on the wrapper as an attribute: `wrapper.calls`. Use `functools.wraps`.

tests.exec:
@count_calls
def add(a, b):
    """Adds."""
    return a + b
assert add(2, 3) == 5 and add(a=1, b=1) == 2, "The function still works, with any arguments"
assert add.calls == 2, f"add.calls should be 2, got {add.calls}"
assert add.__name__ == "add" and add.__doc__ == "Adds.", "Use functools.wraps to keep the name and docstring"
tests.label: Counts calls and keeps the original's name

ex.q: Write `memoize`, a decorator that caches results: if the function was already called with the same arguments, return the saved answer instead of computing again. (Python ships this as `functools.lru_cache`, but build it yourself.) Then decorate the slow recursive `fib` so `fib(80)` is instant.

Decorators can take settings. That needs one more layer: a function that **returns** a decorator. Write `retry(times)`: the decorated function is called again if it raises an exception, up to `times` attempts in total. If every attempt fails, the last exception is raised.

tests.label: Retries until it works
Gives up after the limit and raises

ex.title: Setup and guaranteed cleanup
ex.text:
`with open(...) as f:` guarantees the file is closed, even if an error happens inside. That's a **context manager**: an object with `__enter__` (runs at the start of the `with`) and `__exit__` (always runs at the end). Real uses: files, database transactions, locks, timers, temporarily changing a setting.
The quick way to write one is `@contextlib.contextmanager` around a generator: code before `yield` is setup, code after is cleanup (put it in `finally` so it runs even on errors).

ex.q:
Write a class-based context manager `Timer`. `__enter__` records `time.perf_counter()` and returns the Timer itself; `__exit__` stores the seconds that passed in `self.elapsed`. It must not hide errors (return `False` from `__exit__`).
```
with Timer() as t:
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))
print(t.elapsed)
```

tests.exec:
with Timer() as t:
    sum(range(200_000))
assert isinstance(t, Timer), "__enter__ should return the Timer itself"
assert 0 <= t.elapsed < 5, f"elapsed should be the seconds that passed, got {t.elapsed}"
tests.label: Measures time
Errors still come out

ex.q: Write `temporary(settings, key, value)` with `@contextlib.contextmanager`: inside the `with`, `settings[key]` is `value`; afterwards the old value is restored, **even if an error happened**. If the key didn't exist before, remove it afterwards.

tests.exec:
s = {"theme": "dark"}
with temporary(s, "theme", "light"):
    assert s["theme"] == "light", "Inside the with, the new value is used"
assert s == {"theme": "dark"}, "Afterwards the old value is back"
with temporary(s, "debug", True):
    assert s["debug"] is True
assert "debug" not in s, "A key that didn't exist is removed again"
tests.label: Sets and restores
Restores even after an error

challenge.why: Closures look up `i` when they're called, not when they're made. By then the loop has finished and i is 2. Fix it with `lambda x, i=i: x + i`.

challenge.code:
a = {"tags": ["x"]}
b = dict(a)
b["tags"].append("y")
b["name"] = "copy"
print(a)
challenge.why: dict(a) is a shallow copy. The new dictionary has its own keys, but both share the same tags list.

challenge.q: Write a generator `batched(items, size)` that yields lists of `size` items (the last batch may be smaller). It must work on any iterable, including other generators.
Write a decorator `validate_positive` that raises `ValueError` if any positional argument is a number below zero, and otherwise calls the function normally.

tests.label: Blocks negative numbers

units.title: Python's Toolbox
units.blurb: Modules, dates, smart collections and regular expressions. Stop reinventing what Python already gives you.

ex.title: Batteries included
ex.text:
Python ships with a huge **standard library**. Bring a module in with `import`:
- `import math` then `math.sqrt(2)`
- `from random import choice` then `choice(items)`
- `import statistics as st` to shorten a long name
Any `.py` file is a module too: put functions in `helpers.py` and `import helpers` from the file next to it.
ex.code:
import math, statistics as st
from random import seed, choice, sample

print(math.sqrt(144), math.pi, math.ceil(4.1))
print(st.mean([3, 7, 8]), st.median([3, 7, 8, 100]))
seed(1)
print(choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]), sample(range(1, 50), 6))

ex.title: Your own module
ex.text: Here, `tools.py` is a file in the lesson's folder. The main program imports it like any other module.
ex.code:
import tools
print(tools.slugify("Hello World, From Python!"))
print(tools.VERSION)

ex.q: After `from math import sqrt`, how do you call it?

Write `password(length, seed_value)` that uses `random` (seeded with `random.seed(seed_value)`) to build a password of `length` characters, each picked with `random.choice` from letters + digits + `"!@#$%"`. Use `string.ascii_letters` and `string.digits`.

tests.label: The same seed gives the same password

ex.title: datetime
ex.text:
- `date(2026, 12, 25)` is a calendar date, `datetime` adds a time
- subtracting dates gives a `timedelta`; `.days` is its length
- `timedelta(days=30)` can be added to dates
- `.strftime("%b %d, %Y")` formats; `datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d")` parses
ex.code:
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

launch = date(2026, 12, 25)
today = date(2026, 10, 9)
print((launch - today).days, "days to go")
print(today + timedelta(weeks=6))
print(launch.strftime("%A, %B %d"))
meeting = datetime.strptime("2026-10-14 09:30", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
print(meeting.hour, meeting.strftime("%I:%M %p"))

from datetime import date
print((date(2026, 3, 1) - date(2026, 2, 1)).days)
ex.why: February 2026 has 28 days.

ex.q: Write `age_on(birthday, day)` that returns someone's age in whole years on a given date (both are `date` objects). Count carefully around the birthday itself.
Write `next_birthday(birthday, today)` that returns how many days until the next birthday (0 if it's today). Ignore Feb 29 birthdays.

ex.title: collections
ex.text:
- `Counter` counts anything in one line, and `.most_common(n)` ranks it
- `defaultdict(list)` creates missing keys automatically (no more setdefault)
- `deque` is a list that's fast at both ends, great for queues and "last N items"
- `namedtuple` gives tuples readable field names
ex.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple

words = "to be or not to be that is the question".split()
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))

by_len = defaultdict(list)
for w in words:
    by_len[len(w)].append(w)
print(dict(by_len))

recent = deque(maxlen=3)
for page in ["home", "shop", "cart", "pay"]:
    recent.append(page)
print(list(recent))

Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
p = Point(3, 4)
print(p.x, p)

ex.q: Write `top_hashtags(posts, n)` that returns the n most common hashtags (words starting with `#`, compared in lowercase) across all posts, as a list of `(tag, count)`. Use Counter.

ex.title: itertools
ex.text:
`itertools` builds combinations without nested loops:
- `combinations(items, 2)` every pair (order doesn't matter)
- `permutations(items, 2)` every ordered pair
- `product(a, b)` every combination across lists
- `accumulate(nums)` running totals
ex.code:
from itertools import combinations, product, accumulate
team = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee"]
print(list(combinations(team, 2)))
print(len(list(product("ABC", range(3)))))
print(list(accumulate([5, 10, -3, 8])))

ex.q: Write `pairs_with_sum(nums, target)` that returns every pair `(a, b)` from the list (using each position once, a before b in the list) that adds up to target. Use `itertools.combinations`.

ex.title: Patterns for text
ex.text:
A **regular expression** describes a text pattern. The essentials:
- `\d` digit, `\w` letter/digit/underscore, `\s` space, `.` any character
- `+` one or more, `*` zero or more, `?` optional, `{3}` exactly 3
- `[abc]` any of these, `^` start, `$` end, `( )` capture a group
`re.findall` finds every match; `re.search` finds the first; `re.sub` replaces. Write patterns as raw strings: `r"\d+"`.
ex.code:
import re
text = "Call 555-0142 or 555-0199. Email sam@pyforge.dev or ops@acme.co"
print(re.findall(r"\d{3}-\d{4}", text))
print(re.findall(r"[\w.]+@[\w.]+\.\w+", text))
m = re.search(r"(\w+)@(\w+)", text)
print(m.group(1), m.group(2))
print(re.sub(r"\d", "#", "PIN 4821"))

import re
print(re.findall(r"\d+", "3 cats, 12 dogs, 0 fish"))

ex.q: Write `extract_prices(text)` that returns every dollar price in the text as a float: `"Coffee $4.50, bagel $3, combo $6.75"` gives `[4.5, 3.0, 6.75]`.
Write `is_strong(pw)` with one regex check per rule: at least 10 characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit, and a symbol from `!@#$%^&*`.

challenge.code:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter("banana").most_common(1))

from datetime import date, timedelta
print(date(2026, 12, 30) + timedelta(days=3))

challenge.q: Write `normalize_phone(text)` that pulls the digits out of a US phone number in any format and returns it as `(555) 014-2299`. Return None if there aren't exactly 10 digits (ignore a leading 1 if there are 11).
Write `weekday_counts(dates)` that takes date strings like `"2026-10-09"` and returns a dictionary counting how many fall on each weekday name (`"Friday"` etc.). Use datetime and Counter.
challenge.start:
from datetime import datetime
from collections import Counter

units.title: The Internet & APIs
units.blurb: Pull live data from the web. Weather, currencies, anything with an API.

ex.title: Requests and responses
ex.text:
Every time an app loads data, it sends an **HTTP request** to a URL and gets a **response** back:
- a **status code**: 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 401 Unauthorized, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Server Error
- a **body**, usually JSON for APIs
An **API** is a URL designed for programs instead of people. You ask in the URL (`?city=Paris&units=metric`), it answers in JSON.

ex.q: What does a 404 status code mean?
opts: The thing you asked for doesn't exist at that URL

ex.q: Which status codes mean "your request was fine but you're asking too often"?

ex.title: Building URLs safely
ex.text: Query parameters go after `?`, joined with `&`. Spaces and symbols must be **encoded** (`New York` becomes `New+York`). `urllib.parse.urlencode` does it for you.
ex.code:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
base = "https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search"
params = {"name": "São Paulo", "count": 1, "language": "en"}
print(base + "?" + urlencode(params))

ex.q: Write `forecast_url(lat, lon, days=3)` that returns the Open-Meteo forecast URL: base `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast` with parameters `latitude`, `longitude`, `current` = `temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m`, `daily` = `temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min` and `forecast_days`, in that order.

ex.title: requests in four lines
ex.text:
The `requests` library is how Python talks to the web:
```
r = requests.get(url, params={...}, timeout=10)
r.status_code    # 200?
data = r.json()  # parsed JSON
```
Press **Run** to get live weather for Berlin (you need an internet connection).
ex.code:
import requests
r = requests.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
                 params={"latitude": 52.52, "longitude": 13.41, "current": "temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m"},
                 timeout=10)
print(r.status_code)
now = r.json()["current"]
print(f"Berlin: {now['temperature_2m']}°C, wind {now['wind_speed_10m']} km/h")

ex.title: Separate fetching from parsing
ex.text: Pro tip: keep the network call in one small function and the **parsing** in another that takes plain data. You can test the parsing without the internet, and swap the data source later. The exercises here give you real API responses saved as JSON.

ex.q: `geo.json` is a real response from Open-Meteo's geocoding API. Write `first_place(data)` that returns `(name, country, latitude, longitude)` for the first result, or None if there are no results.

Write `check(response)` that returns the parsed JSON if the status is 200. For 404 raise `LookupError("not found")`, for 429 raise `RuntimeError("rate limited")`, and for anything else raise `RuntimeError(f"HTTP {status}")`. Responses have `.status_code` and `.json()`.

tests.label: Errors become clear exceptions

ex.title: Digging into nested data
ex.text:
API responses are nested dictionaries and lists. Find your way with the keys, and turn the result into the shape **you** need, often a list of small dictionaries or tuples.
Use `.get(key, default)` for fields that might be missing.
ex.code:
import json
data = json.load(open("forecast.json"))
daily = data["daily"]
for day, hi, lo in zip(daily["time"], daily["temperature_2m_max"], daily["temperature_2m_min"]):
    print(f"{day}: {lo:>5}° to {hi:>5}°")

ex.q: Write `daily_summary(data)` for a forecast response like `forecast.json`. Return a list of strings like `"2026-10-10: 8.2–13.4°C, rain"`, using the `WMO` dictionary below to describe each day's `weather_code` (unknown codes say `"unknown"`).

`rates.json` is a currency API response with a `base` and a `rates` dictionary. Write `convert(data, amount, to)` that converts an amount from the base currency, rounded to 2. If `to` is the base itself, return the amount unchanged; for an unknown currency raise `KeyError`.

tests.label: Unknown currencies raise KeyError

ex.q: `repos.json` holds a list of GitHub-style repositories. Write `top_repos(data, n)` that returns the n most-starred repos as `"name (stars★, language)"` strings, skipping archived repos. Missing languages show as `"?"`.
ex.solution:
import json

def top_repos(data, n):
    live = [r for r in data if not r.get("archived")]
    live.sort(key=lambda r: r["stargazers_count"], reverse=True)
    return [f"{r['name']} ({r['stargazers_count']}★, {r.get('language') or '?'})" for r in live[:n]]

ex.title: Things go wrong on networks
ex.text:
Real API code must expect failure:
- always pass a **timeout**, or a slow server can freeze your program forever
- **retry** temporary failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) a few times, waiting longer each time (exponential backoff)
- **cache** answers you'll ask for again
- keep **API keys** out of your code: read them from an environment variable with `os.environ.get("WEATHER_KEY")`

ex.q: Write `with_retries(func, attempts=3)`: call `func()`. If it raises `ConnectionError`, try again, up to `attempts` times in total. Return the first successful result, or raise the last error if every attempt fails. Record each wait in the list `waits` (1, then 2, then 4 seconds) instead of actually sleeping.

tests.label: Retries with backoff, then gives up

ex.q: Write a caching wrapper: `cached_fetch(url, fetch)` returns `fetch(url)`, but remembers results in the dictionary `CACHE` so the same URL is only fetched once.

tests.exec:
hits = []
def fake(url):
    hits.append(url)
    return len(url)
assert cached_fetch("https://a.dev", fake) == 13
assert cached_fetch("https://a.dev", fake) == 13
cached_fetch("https://b.dev/x", fake)
assert hits == ["https://a.dev", "https://b.dev/x"], f"Each URL should be fetched once, fetched {hits}"
tests.label: Repeat requests come from the cache

ex.q: Where should an API key live?
opts: In an environment variable or a secrets file that isn't shared
In the URL you post in a chat

challenge.q: Which status code range means the server failed?

challenge.code:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
print(urlencode({"q": "fish & chips", "page": 2}))

challenge.q: Write `warmest(cities)` where cities is a list of `(name, forecast_json)` pairs. Each forecast has `current.temperature_2m`. Return the name of the warmest city.
challenge.solution:
def warmest(cities):
    return max(cities, key=lambda c: c[1]["current"]["temperature_2m"])[0]

challenge.q: Write `paginate(fetch_page)`: `fetch_page(n)` returns `{"items": [...], "next": n + 1 or None}`. Starting from page 1, collect all items across every page until `next` is None.
challenge.solution:
def paginate(fetch_page):
    items, page = [], 1
    while page is not None:
        data = fetch_page(page)
        items += data["items"]
        page = data["next"]
    return items

tests.exec:
pages = {1: {"items": ["a", "b"], "next": 2}, 2: {"items": ["c"], "next": 3}, 3: {"items": [], "next": None}}
assert paginate(lambda n: pages[n]) == ["a", "b", "c"]
tests.label: Collects items from every page

units.title: Data Analysis
units.blurb: pandas, the tool data analysts use every day. Load, filter, group, chart, and answer real questions.

ex.title: A spreadsheet in Python
ex.text:
A pandas **DataFrame** is a table: named columns, numbered rows. Load one from CSV with `pd.read_csv`, then explore:
- `df.head()` first rows, `df.shape` (rows, columns), `df.columns`
- `df["rating"]` is one column (a **Series**), with `.mean()`, `.max()`, `.sum()`...
- `df.describe()` summarizes every numeric column at once
Loading pandas the first time takes a few seconds.
ex.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df.head(3))

ex.title: Real data is messy

Before analysis comes cleaning:
- `df.isna().sum()` counts missing values; `.fillna(0)` or `.dropna()` deals with them

ex.q: `sales.csv` has some duplicate rows and missing `units`. Write `monthly_revenue(path)`: drop exact duplicates, treat missing units as 0, compute revenue = units × price, and return total revenue per month as a dictionary like `{"2026-07": 1234.5, ...}` (month strings, values rounded to 2).
ex.solution:
import pandas as pd

def monthly_revenue(path):
    df = pd.read_csv(path).drop_duplicates()
    df["units"] = df["units"].fillna(0)
    df["revenue"] = df["units"] * df["price"]
    month = pd.to_datetime(df["date"]).dt.strftime("%Y-%m")
    return df.groupby(month)["revenue"].sum().round(2).to_dict()
