    screen.circle(ball["x"], ball["y"], ball["r"], "white")
    screen.text(f"Score {score}", 16, 16, 22, "white")
    screen.text(f"Level {level + 1}", WIDTH / 2, 16, 22, "#a99fc6", "center")
    for i in range(lives):
        screen.sprite("heart", WIDTH - 30 - i * 28, 28, 20)
    if ball["stuck"] and state == "play":
        screen.text("Press space to launch", WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2 + 60, 22, "#a99fc6", "center")
    if state != "play":
        screen.text("You win!" if state == "won" else "Game over", WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2 - 30, 52, "white", "center")
        screen.text(f"Score {score}   Best {best}   ·   space to play again", WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2 + 30, 20, "#ffc94d", "center")

steps.title: The paddle
steps.text: Write `move_paddle(dt)`: move `paddle_x` (the paddle's **center**) with the arrow keys at 600 px/s, and also follow the mouse or your finger when the screen is touched (`if mouse.down: paddle_x = mouse.x`). Keep the whole paddle on screen.

tests.exec:
paddle_x = 400
keyboard._down = {"right"}
move_paddle(0.1)
assert abs(paddle_x - 460) < 0.01, f"Right arrow for 0.1 s should move to 460, got {paddle_x}"
move_paddle(10)
assert paddle_x == WIDTH - PADDLE_W / 2, "The paddle must stay fully on screen"
keyboard._down = set()
mouse.down, mouse.x = True, 200
move_paddle(0.01)
assert paddle_x == 200, "Touching the screen moves the paddle to your finger"
mouse.down = False
tests.label: Keys and touch move the paddle, which stays on screen

steps.title: Ball physics
steps.text:
Write `move_ball(dt)`. Move the ball by its velocity. Bounce off the left, right and top walls (flip `vx` or `vy`, and push the ball back inside).
If it hits the paddle while moving down, bounce up, and **aim it**: where it lands on the paddle sets the angle. Use `offset = (ball["x"] - paddle_x) / (PADDLE_W / 2)` (from −1 to 1), then `angle = offset * 60` degrees from straight up, keeping the same speed:
`vx = speed * sin(angle)`, `vy = -speed * cos(angle)` (use `math.radians`).
steps.solution:
def move_ball(dt):
    b = ball
    b["x"] += b["vx"] * dt
    b["y"] += b["vy"] * dt
    if b["x"] < b["r"]:
        b["x"], b["vx"] = b["r"], abs(b["vx"])
        sound.play("click")
    elif b["x"] > WIDTH - b["r"]:
        b["x"], b["vx"] = WIDTH - b["r"], -abs(b["vx"])
        sound.play("click")
    if b["y"] < b["r"]:
        b["y"], b["vy"] = b["r"], abs(b["vy"])
        sound.play("click")
    on_paddle = PADDLE_Y - b["r"] <= b["y"] <= PADDLE_Y + PADDLE_H and abs(b["x"] - paddle_x) <= PADDLE_W / 2 + b["r"]
    if on_paddle and b["vy"] > 0:
        speed = math.hypot(b["vx"], b["vy"])
        offset = clamp((b["x"] - paddle_x) / (PADDLE_W / 2), -1, 1)
        angle = math.radians(offset * 60)
        b["vx"], b["vy"] = speed * math.sin(angle), -speed * math.cos(angle)
        b["y"] = PADDLE_Y - b["r"]
        sound.play("hit")

tests.exec:
ball.update({"x": 3, "y": 200, "vx": -300, "vy": 0})
move_ball(0.01)
assert ball["vx"] > 0, "Bounce off the left wall"
ball.update({"x": 400, "y": 3, "vx": 0, "vy": -300})
move_ball(0.01)
assert ball["vy"] > 0, "Bounce off the top"
paddle_x = 400
ball.update({"x": 400, "y": PADDLE_Y - 9, "vx": 0, "vy": 300})
move_ball(0.01)
assert ball["vy"] < 0 and abs(ball["vx"]) < 1, "A hit in the middle goes straight up"
ball.update({"x": 450, "y": PADDLE_Y - 9, "vx": 0, "vy": 300})
move_ball(0.01)
assert ball["vx"] > 100 and abs(math.hypot(ball["vx"], ball["vy"]) - 300) < 1, "A hit on the right side angles right, at the same speed"
tests.label: Walls bounce and the paddle aims the ball

steps.title: Levels from data
steps.text: Write `load_level(rows)`: turn a list of strings into a list of brick dictionaries. Row r, column c becomes a brick at `x = 40 + c * (BRICK_W + GAP)`, `y = TOP + r * (BRICK_H + GAP)` with keys `x`, `y`, `kind` (the letter) and `hits` (how many hits it takes: 3 for `"S"`, steel bricks, and 1 for everything else). Skip dots.

steps.title: Breaking bricks
steps.text:
Write `hit_bricks()`. For each brick that still has hits, check if the ball's circle overlaps it: find the point on the brick closest to the ball's center and see if it's within the radius.
On a hit: take one hit off the brick, add 10 points (50 for the final hit of a steel brick), and bounce. If the ball's center is beside the brick (left or right of it), flip `vx`; otherwise flip `vy`. Only one brick per call, then `return`.
Add `fx.burst` when a brick breaks.

tests.exec:
score = 0
bricks[:] = [{"x": 100, "y": 100, "kind": "R", "hits": 1}]
ball.update({"x": 130, "y": 128, "vx": 50, "vy": -300})
hit_bricks()
assert bricks[0]["hits"] == 0 and score == 10 and ball["vy"] > 0, "Hitting a brick from below breaks it and bounces the ball down"
bricks[:] = [{"x": 100, "y": 100, "kind": "S", "hits": 3}]
ball.update({"x": 95, "y": 110, "vx": 300, "vy": 10})
hit_bricks()
assert bricks[0]["hits"] == 2 and ball["vx"] < 0, "Hitting from the side flips vx; steel needs 3 hits"
bricks[:] = [{"x": 100, "y": 100, "kind": "R", "hits": 1}]
ball.update({"x": 400, "y": 400})
hit_bricks()
assert bricks[0]["hits"] == 1, "No contact, no hit"
bricks[:] = load_level(LEVELS[0])
tests.label: Bricks break and the ball bounces the right way

missions.finale: Three levels, all from a few strings. Make your own levels by adding to LEVELS, or try a power-up that widens the paddle.

missions.title: Flappy
missions.tagline: Gravity, pipes and a state machine. One tap, endless retries.
missions.intro: Flappy games are pure physics plus a state machine: **ready → playing → dead → ready**. Gravity pulls the bird down every frame; a tap gives it an upward kick. Pipes slide left forever.

steps.title: The bird
steps.text:
Write `class Bird` with `x = 200`, `y = HEIGHT / 2`, `vy = 0` and `r = 16`.
- `update(dt)`: add `GRAVITY * dt` to `vy`, then add `vy * dt` to `y`
- `flap()`: set `vy = FLAP` (a negative number means up) and play `"jump"`
- `draw()`: the `"bird"` sprite, size 40, tilted by its speed: angle = `clamp(vy / 10, -30, 70)` degrees

tests.exec:
b = Bird()
b.update(0.1)
assert abs(b.vy - 150) < 0.01 and abs(b.y - (HEIGHT / 2 + 15)) < 0.01, "Gravity speeds the bird up, then it moves"
b.flap()
assert b.vy == FLAP, "flap() sets vy to FLAP"
b.update(0.01)
assert b.y < HEIGHT / 2 + 15, "After a flap the bird rises"
tests.label: Gravity and flapping

steps.title: Pipes
steps.text:
Write `class Pipe(x, gap_y)`: a pair of pipes with a gap of 150 pixels centered on `gap_y`, 70 pixels wide. It has `passed = False` and `alive = True`.
- `update(dt)`: move left at 180 px/s; when it's fully off the left edge, `alive = False`
- `draw()`: two green rectangles, one from the top of the screen down to the gap, one from below the gap to the ground
- `rects()`: return the two rectangles as `(x, y, w, h)` tuples (top first), for collision checks

tests.exec:
p = Pipe(10, 200)
p.update(0.5)
assert p.x == -80 and not p.alive, "It moves left at 180 px/s and dies once off-screen"
tests.label: Pipes slide left and leave

steps.title: Endless pipes
steps.text: Write `spawn(dt)`: count a `spawn_timer` up by dt; every 1.5 seconds add a `Pipe` just off the right edge (`WIDTH + 20`) with a random gap center between 120 and `GROUND - 120`. Then remove dead pipes from the `pipes` list.
steps.solution:
pipes = []
spawn_timer = 0

def spawn(dt):
    global spawn_timer
    spawn_timer += dt
    if spawn_timer >= 1.5:
        spawn_timer -= 1.5
        pipes.append(Pipe(WIDTH + 20, random.uniform(120, GROUND - 120)))
    pipes[:] = [p for p in pipes if p.alive]

tests.exec:
pipes.clear()
spawn_timer = 0
for _ in range(31):
    spawn(0.1)
assert len(pipes) == 2, f"In 3.1 seconds two pipes should appear, got {len(pipes)}"
assert all(120 <= p.gap_y <= GROUND - 120 for p in pipes), "Gaps stay away from the edges"
pipes.clear()
tests.label: A new pipe every 1.5 seconds

steps.title: Crashing
steps.text:
Write `circle_hits_rect(cx, cy, r, rect)`: True if a circle overlaps a rectangle (find the closest point of the rectangle to the circle's center).
Then `crashed(bird)`: True if the bird hits any pipe rectangle, the ground, or flies above the top of the screen.

tests.exec:
b = Bird(); b.y = GROUND
assert crashed(b), "Touching the ground is a crash"
pipes[:] = [Pipe(b.x - 10, 100)]
b.y = 300
assert crashed(b), "Hitting a pipe is a crash"
b.y = 100
assert not crashed(b), "Flying through the gap is fine"
pipes.clear()
tests.label: Pipes, ground and sky are all deadly

steps.title: Ready, play, dead
steps.text:
Write the game's state machine in `update(dt)`, with globals `bird`, `state` (`"ready"`), `score` and `best` (from `load("best", 0)`):
- **ready**: the bird bobs gently (`bird.y = HEIGHT / 2 + sin(t) × 8` works, or just hold still). A tap (`keyboard.pressed("space")` or `mouse.clicked`) flaps and switches to **playing**.
- **playing**: taps flap; update the bird, `spawn(dt)` and update pipes. When a pipe's right edge passes the bird's x for the first time, mark it `passed` and add 1 to `score` (`sound.play("coin")`). If `crashed(bird)`: `fx.shake(12)`, `sound.play("lose")`, save the best score, switch to **dead**.
- **dead**: a tap resets everything (new Bird, no pipes, score 0) and goes back to **ready**.
Clouds drift left at 20 px/s in every state.
steps.stub:
bird = Bird()
state = "ready"
score = 0
best = load("best", 0)

def update(dt):
    pass

tests.exec:
keyboard._new = {"space"}
update(0.016)
keyboard._new = set()
assert state == "playing" and bird.vy < 0, "A tap in the ready state flaps and starts the game"
pipes[:] = [Pipe(bird.x - Pipe.W - 1, bird.y)]
update(0.016)
assert score == 1 and pipes[0].passed, "Passing a pipe scores a point, once"
update(0.016)
assert score == 1, "Each pipe only scores once"
bird.y = GROUND
update(0.016)
assert state == "dead", "Crashing ends the game"
keyboard._new = {"space"}
update(0.016)
keyboard._new = set()
assert state == "ready" and score == 0 and not pipes, "A tap after dying resets the game"
tests.label: The state machine runs the whole game

missions.finale: Three states and a handful of rules. To make it harder, shrink the gap as the score climbs, or speed the pipes up. To make it yours, swap the bird for another sprite.

missions.title: Minesweeper
missions.tagline: Clear the field. Recursion opens up the empty spaces for you.
missions.intro: Tap a square to reveal it. Numbers say how many mines touch that square. When you reveal a square with **zero** mines around it, the game opens all its neighbours, and their neighbours, and so on. That chain reaction is a recursive flood fill, and you're going to write it.

steps.title: Draw the field
steps.text:
Write `draw()`. Cell `(c, r)` is drawn at pixel `(c * SIZE, TOP + r * SIZE)`. Draw:
- hidden cells in one color, revealed cells in a darker one
- a flag sprite on flagged cells (`screen.sprite("flag", ...)`)
- on revealed cells, the number of neighbouring mines `count(cell)` (skip zeros)
- when the game is over, every mine as a `"bomb"` sprite
- a top bar showing mines left, the time, and whether flag mode is on (tap the bar or press F to toggle)

tests.exec:
import forge._game as g
g._cmds.clear()
draw()
rects = [c for c in g._cmds if c[0] == "r"]
assert len(rects) >= COLS * ROWS, f"Draw all {COLS * ROWS} cells, found {len(rects)} rectangles"
assert any(c[0] == "t" for c in g._cmds), "Show the top bar text"
tests.label: The whole field and the top bar are drawn

steps.title: Lay the mines
steps.text:
Write `neighbours(cell)`, returning the up to 8 cells around `(c, r)` that are on the board.
Write `count(cell)`, the number of mines among its neighbours.
Write `lay_mines(safe)`: fill the `mines` set with `MINES` random cells, never placing one on `safe` or its neighbours, so the first tap is always safe. Set `started = True`.

tests.exec:
mines.clear()
lay_mines((7, 4))
assert len(mines) == MINES, f"There should be {MINES} mines"
assert (7, 4) not in mines and not any(n in mines for n in neighbours((7, 4))), "No mines on or next to the first tap"
mines.clear(); mines.update({(1, 1), (2, 1)})
assert count((1, 2)) == 2 and count((5, 5)) == 0, "count() should count neighbouring mines"
mines.clear()
tests.label: Mines avoid the first tap, counts are right

steps.title: Reveal, recursively
steps.text:
Write `reveal(cell)`:
- if it's already revealed or flagged, do nothing
- add it to `revealed`
- if it has **zero** neighbouring mines (and isn't a mine), call `reveal` on every neighbour
That's the chain reaction.

tests.exec:
mines.clear(); revealed.clear(); flags.clear()
mines.add((15, 8))
reveal((0, 0))
assert len(revealed) == COLS * ROWS - 1, f"With one mine in the corner, one tap should open {COLS * ROWS - 1} cells, opened {len(revealed)}"
assert (15, 8) not in revealed, "Never reveal the mine itself through the chain reaction"
mines.clear(); revealed.clear()
tests.label: Empty areas open up in a chain reaction

steps.title: Tap to play
steps.text:
Write `cell_at(x, y)` that turns a screen position into a `(c, r)` cell, or None if it's in the top bar or off the board.
Write `handle_click(x, y)`:
- a tap in the top bar (`y < TOP`) toggles `flag_mode`
- otherwise find the cell. In flag mode, toggle a flag on hidden cells.
- otherwise: on the first tap, `lay_mines(cell)` first. Then if it's a mine, it's game over (`fx.shake`, `sound.play("explode")`). If not, `reveal(cell)`.
- you win when every non-mine cell is revealed: set `won` and `game_over`, and save the best time.

tests.exec:
restart()
handle_click(375, 275)
assert started and len(mines) == MINES, "The first tap lays the mines"
assert len(revealed) >= 1 and not game_over, "The first tap is always safe"
flag_mode = True
target = next(c for c in mines)
handle_click(target[0] * SIZE + 5, TOP + target[1] * SIZE + 5)
assert target in flags, "In flag mode, tapping a hidden cell flags it"
flag_mode = False
restart()
tests.label: Taps reveal, flag and start the game

missions.finale: Every time a big empty area bursts open, that's your recursive `reveal` calling itself dozens of times. Try a bigger board or more mines for a harder game.

missions.title: Platformer
missions.tagline: Run, jump, stomp and reach the flag. Tile collisions, a scrolling camera and enemies.
missions.intro: This is the capstone game: a side-scrolling platformer like the classics. The level is a list of strings, the player obeys gravity, and every wall and floor is a tile the physics must respect. It's the trickiest game in the Arcade, and you have every skill it needs.

steps.title: Read the level
steps.text:
Write `parse_level(rows)` that returns a dictionary describing the level:
- `"solid"`: a set of `(col, row)` tiles that are `#` or `=`
- `"spikes"` and `"coins"`: sets of `(col, row)` for `^` and `C`
- `"enemies"`: a list of pixel positions `(col * TILE, row * TILE)` for each `E`
- `"start"` and `"flag"`: pixel positions for `P` and `F`
- `"width"`: the level's width in pixels
steps.stub:
def parse_level(rows):
    return {"solid": set(), "spikes": set(), "coins": set(), "enemies": [], "start": (40, 320), "flag": (2520, 120), "width": len(rows[0]) * TILE}

steps.title: The player
steps.text:
Write `class Player(x, y)`: a 28 × 34 body (`w`, `h`) with `vx`, `vy`, `on_ground = False` and `facing = 1`.
`control(dt)`:
- left/right sets `vx` to `-SPEED` / `SPEED` (and `facing`); with neither held, slow down: `vx *= 0.8`
- jump (`space` or `up`) only when `on_ground`: `vy = JUMP`, play `"jump"`
- gravity: `vy += GRAVITY * dt`, but never fall faster than 900
`draw(cam_x)`: the `"player"` sprite at its center, shifted left by the camera.

tests.exec:
p = Player(100, 100)
keyboard._down = {"right"}
p.control(0.01)
assert p.vx == SPEED and p.facing == 1, "Right arrow runs right"
keyboard._down = {"space"}
p.control(0.01)
assert p.vy > 0, "No jumping in mid-air"
p.on_ground = True; p.vy = 0
p.control(0.01)
assert p.vy < 0, "Jump when standing on the ground"
p.vy = 5000
p.control(0.1)
assert p.vy == 900, "Falling speed is capped"
keyboard._down = set()
tests.label: Running, jumping and gravity

steps.title: Tile collisions
steps.text:
The hard part. Write `solid_at(px, py)`: True if the pixel is inside a solid tile.
Then `move_and_collide(body, dt)`, moving **one axis at a time**:
1. `body.x += body.vx * dt`. If any corner of the body is now inside a solid tile: moving right, snap the body's right edge to the tile's left edge; moving left, snap to the tile's right edge. Set `vx = 0`.
2. Then `body.y += body.vy * dt` and do the same vertically. Landing on a tile (moving down) sets `on_ground = True`; hitting your head sets `vy = 0`.
Keep the body inside the level horizontally.

tests.exec:
b = Player(80, 300)
b.vy = 500
for _ in range(60):
    move_and_collide(b, 1 / 60)
    b.vy = min(b.vy + GRAVITY / 60, 900)
assert b.on_ground and abs(b.y + b.h - 10 * TILE) < 0.5, f"The player should land on the floor at y = {10 * TILE}, feet at {b.y + b.h}"
b = Player(400, 10 * TILE - 34)
b.vx = 300
for _ in range(30):
    move_and_collide(b, 1 / 60)
    b.vx = 300
assert b.x + b.w <= 12 * TILE + 0.5, "A wall stops the player"
tests.label: Floors catch you and walls stop you

steps.title: The camera
steps.text:
The level is 2,560 pixels wide but the screen is 800. Write `follow_camera(dt)` that keeps a global `cam_x` so the player stays centered, smoothly (`cam_x += (target - cam_x) * min(1, 8 * dt)`), and never shows past either end of the level.
Then write `draw()`: a sky, distant hills that scroll at half speed (parallax), the visible tiles only (columns from `cam_x // TILE` to one screen past it), spikes, spinning coins, the flag, enemies, the player, and a HUD with coins, lives and time.

tests.exec:
player.x = 1500
for _ in range(120):
    follow_camera(1 / 60)
assert abs(cam_x - (1500 + player.w / 2 - WIDTH / 2)) < 2, "The camera centers on the player"
player.x = 0
for _ in range(120):
    follow_camera(1 / 60)
assert cam_x == 0, "The camera never shows past the start of the level"
import forge._game as g
g._cmds.clear()
draw()
assert len(g._cmds) < 600, "Only draw what's on screen"
player.x = level["start"][0]
tests.label: The camera follows smoothly and stays in bounds

steps.title: Coins, spikes, enemies and the flag
steps.text:
Write `class Slime(x, y)`: a 32 × 28 enemy (`alive`, `vx = 60`). Its `update(dt)` uses `move_and_collide` (give it `vy` and gravity too), and turns around when it hits a wall or would walk off a ledge (no solid tile ahead under its feet). `draw(cam_x)` uses the `"slime"` sprite.
Then write `interact()`:
- touching a coin tile removes it from `coins`, adds 1 to `score`, plays `"coin"`
- touching a spike or falling off the bottom: lose a life and `respawn()` (game over at 0 lives: `state = "lost"`)
- touching a slime: if you're falling onto it (`player.vy > 0` and your feet are near its top), it dies and you bounce (`vy = JUMP * 0.6`); otherwise you get hurt like a spike
- reaching the flag: `state = "won"`, save the best time

tests.exec:
restart()
cell = next(iter(coins))
player.x, player.y = cell[0] * TILE + 6, cell[1] * TILE + 3
interact()
assert score == 1 and cell not in coins, "Touching a coin collects it"
c, r = next(iter(level["spikes"]))
player.x, player.y = c * TILE + 6, r * TILE + 6
interact()
assert lives == 2 and (player.x, player.y) == level["start"], "Spikes cost a life and send you back to the start"
e = enemies[0]
player.x, player.y, player.vy = e.x, e.y - player.h + 6, 300
interact()
assert not e.alive and player.vy < 0, "Landing on a slime stomps it and bounces you"
fx_, fy_ = level["flag"]
player.x, player.y = fx_, fy_
interact()
assert state == "won", "Reaching the flag wins"
restart()
tests.label: Coins, hazards, stomps and the finish line

missions.finale: You built a platformer from nothing: level data, physics, collision, a camera and enemy AI. Design a second level by adding strings to LEVEL, or add double-jump, moving platforms, or a boss.

missions.title: Pong
missions.tagline: The game that started it all. You write every rule.
missions.intro:
Pong is a ball, two paddles and a few rules. A game runs `update(dt)` and then `draw()` about 60 times a second. `dt` is the time since the last frame in seconds, so speeds are in pixels per second.
The starting code sets up the game's variables. You'll write the functions that bring it to life.
missions.scaffold:
from forge import *

WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 500
TITLE = "Pong"
CONTROLS = ["up", "down", "space"]
PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H = 14, 90
BALL_R = 9
WIN_SCORE = 7

player_y = HEIGHT / 2 - PADDLE_H / 2
cpu_y = HEIGHT / 2 - PADDLE_H / 2
ball_x, ball_y = WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2
ball_vx, ball_vy = 330, 160
player_score = 0
cpu_score = 0
game_over = False


def reset_ball(direction):
    global ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx, ball_vy
    ball_x, ball_y = WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2
    ball_vx = 330 * direction
    ball_vy = 160 if ball_vy > 0 else -160


{{draw}}


{{move_player}}


{{move_ball}}


{{paddles}}


{{score}}


{{cpu}}


def update(dt):
    global player_score, cpu_score, game_over
    if game_over:
        if keyboard.pressed("space"):
            player_score = cpu_score = 0
            game_over = False
            reset_ball(1)
        return
    move_player(dt)
    move_cpu(dt)
    move_ball(dt)
    hit_paddles()
    check_score()
    if player_score >= WIN_SCORE or cpu_score >= WIN_SCORE:
        game_over = True

steps.title: Draw the court
steps.text:
Write `draw()`. It should:
- clear the screen (`screen.clear("#0d0b1a")`)
- draw a dashed line down the middle (short rectangles every 30 pixels)
- draw the player's paddle at x = 30, y = `player_y`, and the computer's at x = `WIDTH - 30 - PADDLE_W`, y = `cpu_y`, both `PADDLE_W` × `PADDLE_H`
- draw the ball as a circle at (`ball_x`, `ball_y`) with radius `BALL_R`
- show both scores with `screen.text`
Press **Run** to see the frozen court.
steps.solution:
def draw():
    screen.clear("#0d0b1a")
    for y in range(10, HEIGHT, 30):
        screen.rect(WIDTH / 2 - 2, y, 4, 16, "#2b2441")
    screen.rect(30, player_y, PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H, "#6fd3ff", radius=6)
    screen.rect(WIDTH - 30 - PADDLE_W, cpu_y, PADDLE_W, PADDLE_H, "#ff5c8a", radius=6)
    screen.circle(ball_x, ball_y, BALL_R * 2.2, "rgba(255, 201, 77, 0.15)")
    screen.circle(ball_x, ball_y, BALL_R, "#ffc94d")
    screen.text(player_score, WIDTH / 2 - 60, 24, 56, "#6fd3ff", "right")
    screen.text(cpu_score, WIDTH / 2 + 60, 24, 56, "#ff5c8a", "left")
    if game_over:
        winner = "You win!" if player_score > cpu_score else "Computer wins"
        screen.text(winner, WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2 - 40, 48, "white", "center")
        screen.text("Press space to play again", WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2 + 20, 22, "#a99fc6", "center")

tests.exec:
import forge._game as g
g._cmds.clear()
draw()
kinds = [c[0] for c in g._cmds]
assert kinds[0] == "clear", "Start draw() with screen.clear(...)"
rects = [c for c in g._cmds if c[0] == "r"]
assert any(abs(c[1] - 30) < 1 and abs(c[2] - player_y) < 1 for c in rects), "Draw the player paddle at x = 30, y = player_y"
assert any(abs(c[1] - (WIDTH - 30 - PADDLE_W)) < 1 and abs(c[2] - cpu_y) < 1 for c in rects), "Draw the computer paddle at x = WIDTH - 30 - PADDLE_W, y = cpu_y"
assert any(c[0] == "c" and abs(c[1] - ball_x) < 1 and abs(c[2] - ball_y) < 1 for c in g._cmds), "Draw the ball at (ball_x, ball_y)"
assert any(c[0] == "t" for c in g._cmds), "Show the scores with screen.text(...)"
tests.label: Court, paddles, ball and scores are drawn

hints: screen.rect(x, y, width, height, color) and screen.circle(x, y, radius, color)
screen.text(player_score, x, y, size, color) shows a number.

steps.title: Move your paddle
steps.text:
Write `move_player(dt)`. While `keyboard.up` is held, move `player_y` up by 420 pixels per second (that's `420 * dt` this frame); while `keyboard.down` is held, move it down.
Keep the paddle on screen: `player_y` must stay between 0 and `HEIGHT - PADDLE_H`. The built-in `clamp(value, low, high)` helps.
Remember `global player_y`.

tests.exec:
player_y = 200
keyboard._down = {"up"}
move_player(0.1)
assert abs(player_y - 158) < 0.01, f"Holding up for 0.1 s should move from 200 to 158, got {player_y}"
keyboard._down = {"down"}
move_player(0.1)
assert abs(player_y - 200) < 0.01, "Holding down should move the paddle down"
keyboard._down = {"up"}
move_player(5)
assert player_y == 0, "The paddle shouldn't leave the top of the screen"
keyboard._down = {"down"}
move_player(5)
assert player_y == HEIGHT - PADDLE_H, "The paddle shouldn't leave the bottom of the screen"
keyboard._down = set()
tests.label: The paddle moves and stays on screen

steps.title: Get the ball moving
steps.text:
Write `move_ball(dt)`. Move the ball by its velocity (`ball_vx * dt` and `ball_vy * dt`).
If it hits the top (`ball_y - BALL_R < 0`), put it back at `BALL_R` and make `ball_vy` positive. If it hits the bottom, put it at `HEIGHT - BALL_R` and make `ball_vy` negative. Play `sound.play("hit")` on each bounce.
steps.solution:
def move_ball(dt):
    global ball_x, ball_y, ball_vy
    ball_x += ball_vx * dt
    ball_y += ball_vy * dt
    if ball_y - BALL_R < 0:
        ball_y = BALL_R
        ball_vy = abs(ball_vy)
        sound.play("hit")
    elif ball_y + BALL_R > HEIGHT:
        ball_y = HEIGHT - BALL_R
        ball_vy = -abs(ball_vy)
        sound.play("hit")

tests.exec:
ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx, ball_vy = 400, 250, 300, 100
move_ball(0.5)
assert (ball_x, ball_y) == (550, 300), f"After 0.5 s the ball should be at (550, 300), got ({ball_x}, {ball_y})"
ball_y, ball_vy = 5, -200
move_ball(0.1)
assert ball_vy > 0 and ball_y >= BALL_R, "Bounce off the top: ball_vy should become positive"
ball_y, ball_vy = HEIGHT - 3, 200
move_ball(0.1)
assert ball_vy < 0 and ball_y <= HEIGHT - BALL_R, "Bounce off the bottom: ball_vy should become negative"
tests.label: The ball moves and bounces off the walls

steps.title: Hit the paddles
steps.text:
Write `hit_paddles()`. If the ball is moving left (`ball_vx < 0`), its left edge (`ball_x - BALL_R`) has reached the player's paddle (x ≤ `30 + PADDLE_W`), and `ball_y` is between `player_y` and `player_y + PADDLE_H`: send it right with `ball_vx = abs(ball_vx) * 1.05` (5% faster each hit).
Do the same for the computer paddle on the right (`ball_x + BALL_R >= WIDTH - 30 - PADDLE_W`).
Bonus feel: add `fx.burst(ball_x, ball_y, "#6fd3ff")` and `sound.play("hit")`, and add spin with `ball_vy += (ball_y - (player_y + PADDLE_H / 2)) * 5`.
steps.solution:
def hit_paddles():
    global ball_vx, ball_vy
    if ball_vx < 0 and ball_x - BALL_R <= 30 + PADDLE_W and player_y <= ball_y <= player_y + PADDLE_H:
        ball_vx = abs(ball_vx) * 1.05
        ball_vy += (ball_y - (player_y + PADDLE_H / 2)) * 5
        fx.burst(ball_x, ball_y, "#6fd3ff")
        sound.play("hit")
    if ball_vx > 0 and ball_x + BALL_R >= WIDTH - 30 - PADDLE_W and cpu_y <= ball_y <= cpu_y + PADDLE_H:
        ball_vx = -abs(ball_vx) * 1.05
        ball_vy += (ball_y - (cpu_y + PADDLE_H / 2)) * 5
        fx.burst(ball_x, ball_y, "#ff5c8a")
        sound.play("hit")

tests.exec:
player_y = 200
ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx, ball_vy = 50, 245, -300, 0
hit_paddles()
assert ball_vx > 0, "A ball touching your paddle should bounce to the right"
assert abs(ball_vx - 315) < 0.01, "It should speed up by 5% (300 → 315)"
ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx = 50, 100, -300
hit_paddles()
assert ball_vx < 0, "If the ball misses the paddle (above it), it keeps going"
cpu_y = 200
ball_x, ball_y, ball_vx = WIDTH - 50, 250, 300
hit_paddles()
assert ball_vx < 0, "The computer's paddle should bounce the ball back left"
tests.label: Both paddles bounce the ball

steps.title: Keep score
steps.text:
Write `check_score()`. If the ball goes past the left edge (`ball_x < -20`), the computer scores: add 1 to `cpu_score` and call `reset_ball(1)`. If it goes past the right edge (`ball_x > WIDTH + 20`), you score and call `reset_ball(-1)`.
Add `fx.shake(10)` and a sound for drama.
steps.solution:
def check_score():
    global player_score, cpu_score
    if ball_x < -20:
        cpu_score += 1
        fx.shake(10)
        sound.play("lose")
        reset_ball(1)

missions.title: Star Shooter

missions.intro: A real game is a crowd of objects: a player, bullets, enemies, power-ups. Each one knows how to `update(dt)` itself and `draw()` itself, and the game loop just asks all of them to do it. You'll write each class.

Write `handle_collisions()`:

bullets[:] = [Bullet(305, 205, -500)]

steps.title: Waves
steps.text:
Write `spawn_wave(n)` that returns a list of enemies for wave n:
- a grid of aliens with `min(1 + n // 2, 4)` rows and 8 columns
- the alien in column c, row r goes at x = 120 + c × 80, y = 70 + r × 50
- plus `min(n // 2, 3)` UFOs along the top (y = 40), at x = 160, 400 and 640

steps.title: Power-ups
steps.text:
Write `class PowerUp(x, y)` with `alive = True`: it falls at 90 px/s (dies off-screen), draws as a spinning `"bolt"` sprite, and `collect(player)` gives the player 6 seconds of triple shot (`player.triple_until = 6`) and plays `"powerup"`.

tests.label: Power-ups fall and grant triple shot

missions.finale: Six classes, one loop that asks every object to update and draw itself. That's how almost every game engine works. Ideas: a boss every 5 waves, shields, or a second weapon.

missions.title: Snake
missions.tagline: Eat, grow, don't bite yourself. Lists and grids in motion.
missions.intro: The snake is just a **list of grid cells**, head first. Each tick, add a new head in the direction you're moving and drop the tail, unless you just ate. That's the whole trick.
missions.scaffold:
from forge import *
import random

CELL = 25
COLS, ROWS = 32, 20
WIDTH, HEIGHT = COLS * CELL, ROWS * CELL
TITLE = "Snake"
CONTROLS = ["left", "right", "up", "down", "space"]

snake = [(8, 10), (7, 10), (6, 10)]
direction = (1, 0)
next_direction = (1, 0)
food = (20, 10)
score = 0
best = load("best", 0)
timer = 0
speed = 0.11
game_over = False


{{draw}}


{{turn}}


{{next_head}}


{{food}}


{{step}}


def restart():
    global snake, direction, next_direction, score, timer, speed, game_over
    snake = [(8, 10), (7, 10), (6, 10)]
    direction = next_direction = (1, 0)
    score, timer, speed, game_over = 0, 0, 0.11, False
    place_food()


def update(dt):
    global timer
    if game_over:
        if keyboard.pressed("space"):
            restart()
        return
    turn()
    timer += dt
    if timer >= speed:
        timer -= speed
        step()

steps.title: Draw the snake
steps.text:
Write `draw()`. Clear the screen, then draw:
- the food as a sprite: `screen.sprite("gem", fx, fy, 22, 0, "#ff5c8a")` at the center of its cell
- every snake segment as a rounded square: cell `(x, y)` sits at pixel `(x * CELL, y * CELL)`. Make it `CELL - 2` wide so the segments have gaps, and `radius=6`.
- the score in the corner
Use a brighter color for the head (`snake[0]`).

tests.exec:

g._cmds.clear()
draw()
rects = [c for c in g._cmds if c[0] == "r"]
for x, y in snake:
    assert any(abs(c[1] - (x * CELL + 1)) <= 1.01 and abs(c[2] - (y * CELL + 1)) <= 1.01 for c in rects), f"No segment drawn for cell ({x}, {y}). It should be near pixel ({x * CELL}, {y * CELL})"
assert any(c[0] == "s" for c in g._cmds), "Draw the food with screen.sprite"
tests.label: Every segment and the food are drawn

steps.title: Steer
steps.text:
Write `turn()`. Read the arrow keys and set `next_direction`: left is `(-1, 0)`, right `(1, 0)`, up `(0, -1)`, down `(0, 1)`.
A snake can't reverse into itself: ignore a key that points exactly opposite the current `direction`.

tests.exec:
direction = (1, 0); next_direction = (1, 0)
keyboard._down = {"up"}
turn()
assert next_direction == (0, -1), "Up arrow should set next_direction to (0, -1)"
keyboard._down = {"left"}
turn()
assert next_direction == (0, -1), "Moving right, pressing left must be ignored (no U-turns)"
keyboard._down = set()
tests.label: Arrow keys steer, with no U-turns

steps.title: Where's the head going?
steps.text:
Write `next_head(head, d)` that returns the cell one step from `head` in direction `d`. `next_head((5, 5), (1, 0))` is `(6, 5)`.
Then write `hits(cell)` that returns True if the cell is outside the grid or part of the snake.

steps.title: Food
steps.text: Write `place_food()`: pick a random cell (`random.randrange(COLS)`, `random.randrange(ROWS)`) that isn't part of the snake and store it in the global `food`. Keep trying until you find a free one.

tests.exec:
snake = [(x, y) for x in range(COLS) for y in range(ROWS) if (x, y) != (3, 4)]
place_food()
assert food == (3, 4), "With only one free cell left, food has to go there"
snake = [(8, 10), (7, 10), (6, 10)]
for _ in range(50):
    place_food()
    assert food not in snake and 0 <= food[0] < COLS and 0 <= food[1] < ROWS, "Food must be on the grid and not on the snake"
tests.label: Food lands on a free cell

steps.title: Move, eat, grow
steps.text:
Write `step()`, one tick of the game:
1. `direction = next_direction`, and work out the new head
2. If the new head `hits` something: set `game_over = True`, save the best score with `save("best", best)` if you beat it, play a sound and return
3. Insert the new head at the front of `snake`
4. If it's on the food: add 1 to `score`, `place_food()`, and make the game a little faster (`speed *= 0.97`). Otherwise remove the tail with `snake.pop()`
steps.solution:
def step():
    global direction, score, speed, game_over, best
    direction = next_direction
    head = next_head(snake[0], direction)
    if hits(head):
        game_over = True
        fx.shake(12)
        sound.play("lose")
        if score > best:
            best = score
            save("best", best)
        return
    snake.insert(0, head)
    if head == food:
        score += 1
        speed *= 0.97
        sound.play("coin")
        fx.burst(head[0] * CELL + CELL / 2, head[1] * CELL + CELL / 2, "#ff5c8a")
        place_food()
    else:
        snake.pop()

tests.exec:
snake = [(8, 10), (7, 10), (6, 10)]
direction = next_direction = (1, 0)
food = (20, 10); score = 0; game_over = False
step()
assert snake == [(9, 10), (8, 10), (7, 10)], f"After one step right the snake should be [(9, 10), (8, 10), (7, 10)], got {snake}"
food = (10, 10)
step()
assert len(snake) == 4 and score == 1, "Eating food grows the snake by one and adds 1 to score"
snake = [(COLS - 1, 5), (COLS - 2, 5)]
direction = next_direction = (1, 0)
step()
assert game_over, "Hitting the right wall ends the game"
tests.label: The snake moves, eats, grows and crashes

missions.finale: The whole snake is a list, and the game is three list operations: insert a head, pop a tail, check membership. Try adding walls, a second food type, or wrap-around edges.

missions.intro: **A maintenance job.** Most programmers spend more time changing existing code than writing new code. A shop's inventory program has been running for months. steps.title: The feature request

*"Can the morning report flag anything that's running low? And at the bottom, give me a reorder list, lowest stock first, like `Reorder: Mug (3 left), Backpack (5 left)`. If nothing is low, leave that line out."*

Update `report(inv, threshold=5)`: add `  LOW` (two spaces, then LOW) at the end of each low-stock row, and the `Reorder:` line after the total. Reuse `low_stock()` rather than writing the rule again: one rule, one place.
steps.stub:
def report(inv):
    """The daily stock report the shop owner reads every morning."""
    print(f"{'SKU':<6}{'Item':<14}{'Qty':>5}{'Value':>10}")
    for sku in sorted(inv.items):

steps.solution:
def report(inv, threshold=5):
    """The daily stock report the shop owner reads every morning."""
    low = inv.low_stock(threshold)
    print(f"{'SKU':<6}{'Item':<14}{'Qty':>5}{'Value':>10}")
    for sku in sorted(inv.items):
        item = inv.items[sku]
        value = item["qty"] * item["price"]
        flag = "  LOW" if sku in low else ""
        print(f"{sku:<6}{item['name']:<14}{item['qty']:>5}{value:>10.2f}{flag}")
    print(f"Total stock value: {inv.total_value():.2f}")
    if low:
        print("Reorder: " + ", ".join(f"{inv.items[sku]['name']} ({inv.items[sku]['qty']} left)" for sku in low))

missions.title: Maintenance Job: Untangle the Order Script
missions.tagline: Write tests first, then refactor messy working code into clean functions without changing what it does.
missions.intro: **A maintenance job.** A small business runs this script every evening to total the day's orders. It works (mostly), but it's one long function with cryptic names and global variables, and nobody dares to touch it. The professional way to fix code like this: **first write tests** that pin down how it should behave, **then refactor** in small steps, re-running the tests each time. If they stay green, you didn't break anything.
missions.scaffold:
{{code}}


{{tests}}


SAMPLE = """# orders exported 2026-10-09
Ava; mug:2:8.00, pen:10:1.25
Ben; backpack:1:42.00; SAVE10

Cy; notebook:4:3.50, mug:1:8.00; HALF
Dee; lamp:1:24.50; BOGUS"""

print(process(SAMPLE))

steps.title: Tests first
steps.text:
Read `process()` (use **Step** to watch it), then write **at least 3** pytest-style test functions (`def test_...():` with `assert`) that describe how it should behave. Ideas: one simple order, a discount code, comments and blank lines being skipped, an unknown discount code being ignored.

The owner also reported: *"If I run the totals a second time, everything doubles."* Your tests are checked twice:
- against a **correct** version of the script: they must all pass
- against the **current** script: at least one must **fail**, proving your tests catch the bug

Hint: the demo at the bottom has already run `process` once, so calling it again in a test shows the bug.

tests.label: Your tests pass on correct code
Your tests catch the bug

steps.title: Refactor
steps.text:
Now rewrite the script, keeping `process(text)` working exactly the same way for a single run, but:
- **no global variables** that change (constants like `TAX` and `DISCOUNTS` are fine), so running it twice gives the same answer
- split it into small, named functions, each at most 15 lines:
  - `parse_order(raw)` turns one line into `{"name": ..., "items": [(item, qty, price), ...], "code": ... or None}`
  - `order_subtotal(order)` adds up the items and applies any discount code
  - `process(text)` puts it together
- use clear names (no `p`, `s`, `t`)

Your tests from step 1 must still pass.
steps.stub:
DISCOUNTS = {"SAVE10": 0.10, "HALF": 0.50}
TAX = 0.08
total = 0
count = 0
lines = []

def process(text):
    global total, count, lines
    for raw in text.strip().split("\n"):
        if raw.strip() == "" or raw.startswith("#"):
            continue
        p = raw.split(";")
        n = p[0].strip()
        items = p[1].split(",")
        s = 0
        for it in items:
            nm, q, pr = it.split(":")
            s = s + int(q) * float(pr)
        if len(p) > 2 and p[2].strip() in DISCOUNTS:
            s = s - s * DISCOUNTS[p[2].strip()]
        t = s * TAX
        lines.append(n + ": " + str(round(s, 2)) + " + tax " + str(round(t, 2)) + " = " + str(round(s + t, 2)))
        total = total + s + t
        count = count + 1
    lines.append("Orders: " + str(count) + ", total " + str(round(total, 2)))
    return "\n".join(lines)

tests.exec:
first, second = process(SAMPLE), process(SAMPLE)
assert first == second, "Running it twice must give the same result"
tests.label: Bug fixed: no doubling

tests.exec:
import dis
for name in ("parse_order", "order_subtotal", "process"):
    fn = globals()[name]
    lines = [l for _, _, l in fn.__code__.co_lines() if l]
    length = max(lines) - fn.__code__.co_firstlineno + 1
    assert length <= 15, f"{name}() is {length} lines long; keep each function to 15 lines or fewer"
    stores = [i.argval for i in dis.get_instructions(fn) if i.opname == "STORE_GLOBAL"]
    assert not stores, f"{name}() still changes global variables: {stores}"
tests.label: Small functions, no global state
Your tests from step 1 still pass

missions.finale: That's how professionals change scary code: pin the behavior with tests, then refactor in small safe steps. The new version is shorter, each piece can be tested on its own, and the doubling bug simply disappeared once the global state was gone.

steps.text:
Write the decorator factory `route(method, path)`. A path can contain placeholders like `/notes/<id>`. Turn it into a regular expression where each `<name>` becomes a named group matching anything except `/`: `re.sub(r"<(\w+)>", r"(?P<\1>[^/]+)", path)`, anchored with `^...$`. Append `(method, compiled_regex, fn)` to `ROUTES` and return `fn` unchanged.
Then write `match(method, path)`: return `(fn, params_dict)` for the first route whose method and pattern match, or `None`.

tests.exec:
saved = list(ROUTES)
ROUTES.clear()
@route("GET", "/users/<user_id>/posts/<post_id>")
def get_post(req):
    return "post"
assert get_post({}) == "post", "The decorated function is returned unchanged"
found = match("GET", "/users/7/posts/42")
assert found and found[0] is get_post and found[1] == {"user_id": "7", "post_id": "42"}, f"Got {found}"
assert match("GET", "/users/7/posts") is None, "Paths must match completely"
assert match("POST", "/users/7/posts/42") is None, "The method must match too"
ROUTES[:] = saved
tests.label: Routes with placeholders

steps.title: Handle a request
steps.text:
Write `handle(method, path, body=None)` that returns `(status, data)`:
1. Split off a query string: `path, _, qs = path.partition("?")`, and turn `qs` into a simple dict with `{k: v[0] for k, v in parse_qs(qs).items()}`.
2. Find the route with `match`. None found: if **another method** matches this path, return `405, {"error": "method not allowed"}`; otherwise `404, {"error": "not found"}`.
3. Call the handler with one argument, a request dict: `{"params": ..., "query": ..., "body": body}`. A handler returns either data (meaning status 200) or a `(status, data)` tuple.
4. If the handler raises `ValueError`, return `400, {"error": str(e)}`. Any other exception: `500, {"error": "server error"}` (never leak details to users).
steps.stub:
def handle(method, path, body=None):
    return 404, {"error": "not found"}

tests.label: Dispatch, status codes and errors

steps.title: The database
steps.text:
Write `init_db()`: connect to an in-memory database (store it in a global `DB`), set `DB.row_factory = sqlite3.Row`, and create `notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, text TEXT NOT NULL, done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)`.
Then `note_dict(row)`: turn a row into `{"id": ..., "text": ..., "done": True/False}` (SQLite stores booleans as 0/1, so convert with `bool`).
And `get_note(note_id)`: the note's dict, or `None`.

tests.exec:
init_db()
DB.execute("INSERT INTO notes (text) VALUES ('hello')")
assert get_note(1) == {"id": 1, "text": "hello", "done": False}, f"get_note(1) gave {get_note(1)}"
assert get_note(2) is None
init_db()
assert get_note(1) is None, "init_db starts a fresh database"
tests.label: Notes are stored and read back

steps.title: The endpoints
steps.text:
Now the API itself, using `@route`:
- `GET /notes`: all notes in id order. With `?q=word`, only notes whose text contains it (`LIKE`, with a `?` placeholder!)
- `POST /notes`: body `{"text": ...}`. Blank or missing text: `raise ValueError("text is required")`. Otherwise insert and return `201` with the new note
- `GET /notes/<id>`: the note, or `404, {"error": "note not found"}`
- `PATCH /notes/<id>`: body like `{"done": true}` updates `done` (and/or `text`); return the updated note, or 404
- `DELETE /notes/<id>`: `204, None` if it existed, else 404

Remember: URL params arrive as strings, so convert ids with `int()`.

tests.exec:
init_db()
assert handle("GET", "/notes") == (200, []), "No notes yet"
s, n = handle("POST", "/notes", {"text": "  Water plants "})
assert (s, n) == (201, {"id": 1, "text": "Water plants", "done": False}), f"POST gave {(s, n)}"
handle("POST", "/notes", {"text": "Email Ana"})
assert handle("POST", "/notes", {"text": "   "}) == (400, {"error": "text is required"})
assert handle("POST", "/notes", None)[0] == 400, "A missing body is a 400, not a crash"
assert handle("GET", "/notes/2") == (200, {"id": 2, "text": "Email Ana", "done": False})
assert handle("GET", "/notes/9") == (404, {"error": "note not found"})
assert handle("PATCH", "/notes/1", {"done": True})[1]["done"] is True
assert [x["id"] for x in handle("GET", "/notes?q=ana")[1]] == [2], "Search with ?q="
assert handle("DELETE", "/notes/1") == (204, None)
assert handle("DELETE", "/notes/1")[0] == 404, "Deleting twice is a 404"
assert handle("GET", "/notes?q=' OR '1'='1") == (200, []), "Search must be safe from SQL injection"
tests.label: The whole API behaves
The demo requests

missions.finale: You built a REST API from scratch. In a real framework your code barely changes: Flask spells it `@app.route("/notes/<int:id>", methods=["GET"])` and FastAPI `@app.get("/notes/{id}")`, and they run the web server and turn your return values into HTTP for you. On your laptop: `pip install flask`, paste these endpoints in, and your notes API is live at `http://localhost:5000`.

missions.title: Mini Bank
missions.tagline: Accounts, savings with interest, transfers and statements, built with classes.
missions.intro: Banking software is a classic object-oriented design: accounts know their balance and history, special accounts change a few rules, and a bank coordinates them. You'll build it piece by piece.

steps.title: The Account class
steps.text:
Write `Account(owner)`:
- `balance` starts at 0; `history` is a list of `(kind, amount)` tuples
- `deposit(amount)`: amount must be positive (else ValueError); adds it and records `("deposit", amount)`
- `withdraw(amount)`: positive too; raise `InsufficientFunds` if it's more than the balance; records `("withdraw", amount)`
- `__str__` returns like `Ana: $120.50`

tests.label: Deposits, withdrawals, guards and history

steps.title: Savings accounts
steps.text:
Write `SavingsAccount(owner, rate)` that inherits from Account:
- `add_interest()` deposits one month of interest: balance × rate / 12, rounded to 2 decimals (rate is yearly, like 0.04)
- savings accounts allow at most **3 withdrawals**; the 4th raises `InsufficientFunds("withdrawal limit reached")`

tests.label: Interest and the withdrawal limit

steps.title: The bank
steps.text:
Write `Bank` that manages accounts:
- `open(account)` stores it by owner name (a dict)
- `transfer(from_owner, to_owner, amount)` withdraws from one and deposits to the other. If the withdrawal fails, nothing changes and the error is raised again.
- `total()` is the sum of all balances, rounded to 2
- `report()` returns lines like `Ana: $120.50`, richest first

tests.exec:
b = Bank()
a, c = Account("Ana"), Account("Cy")
b.open(a); b.open(c)
a.deposit(100)
b.transfer("Ana", "Cy", 40)
assert a.balance == 60 and c.balance == 40 and b.total() == 100
try:
    b.transfer("Ana", "Cy", 500)
except InsufficientFunds:
    pass
assert a.balance == 60 and c.balance == 40, "A failed transfer changes nothing"
assert b.report() == ["Ana: $60.00", "Cy: $40.00"]
tests.label: Transfers are all-or-nothing

steps.title: Run the bank
steps.text: Put it to work. Open an `Account("Ana")` with a 2,500 deposit and a `SavingsAccount("Ben", 0.045)` with a 10,000 deposit. Add one month of interest to Ben, transfer 300 from Ana to Ben, then print the report lines and `Total: $12,537.50`.
steps.solution:
bank = Bank()
ana = Account("Ana")
ben = SavingsAccount("Ben", 0.045)
bank.open(ana)
bank.open(ben)
ana.deposit(2500)
ben.deposit(10000)
ben.add_interest()
bank.transfer("Ana", "Ben", 300)
for line in bank.report():
    print(line)
print(f"Total: ${bank.total():,.2f}")

missions.finale: You used every big idea of object-oriented design: encapsulation (accounts guard their own balance), inheritance (savings changes two rules), and composition (the bank holds accounts).

missions.title: Calculator App
missions.tagline: A phone-style calculator, with the logic tested before a single button exists.
missions.intro: A calculator looks simple until you build one: what happens when you press `5 + 3 × 2 =`? Or `=` twice? You'll write the logic as a class first, test it, then put a screen on it.

steps.title: Typing numbers
steps.text:
Write `class Calc` with:
- `current` (the number being typed, as a string, starts `"0"`), `stored` (None), `op` (None) and `fresh` (True: the next digit starts a new number)
- `digit(d)`: append the digit (a string like `"7"`). If `fresh`, replace `current` instead and set `fresh` to False. Don't allow leading zeros like `"007"`. Limit to 12 digits.
- `dot()`: add a decimal point if there isn't one yet (`"0."` if starting fresh)
- `clear()`: back to the start

tests.exec:
c = Calc()
for d in "0072":
    c.digit(d)
assert c.current == "72", f"Leading zeros are dropped: expected 72, got {c.current}"
c.dot(); c.digit("5"); c.dot(); c.digit("1")
assert c.current == "72.51", f"Only one decimal point: expected 72.51, got {c.current}"
c.clear(); c.dot(); c.digit("3")
assert c.current == "0.3"
tests.label: Typing digits and decimal points works

steps.title: Operators and equals
steps.text:
Add methods to `Calc` (as functions that take `self`, then attach them, or edit the class above):
- `operator(op)` for `"+"`, `"−"`, `"×"`, `"÷"`: if there's already a pending operation and you've typed a new number, calculate it first (so `5 + 3 ×` shows 8). Then store the current value, remember the op, and set `fresh`.
- `equals()`: apply the pending op to `stored` and `current`, put the result in `current`, clear `op`. Dividing by zero shows `"Error"`.
Write the arithmetic in a helper `apply(a, op, b)` that returns a float.
steps.stub:
def apply(a, op, b):
    return b

tests.label: Operations chain left to right, and ÷0 shows Error

steps.title: A clean display
steps.text: Write `pretty(text)` for the screen: `"42.0"` shows as `42`, long decimals are rounded to 10 significant digits (`0.1 + 0.2` shows `0.3`), big numbers get commas (`1234567` shows `1,234,567`), and `"Error"` stays `"Error"`. Keep a trailing `"."` or `"0."` while someone is typing.

steps.title: The keypad
steps.text:
Build the app: a big `screen` label (size 48, right-aligned) and rows of buttons like a phone calculator:
```
C   ±   %   ÷
7   8   9   ×
4   5   6   −
1   2   3   +
0   .   =
```
Each button calls `press(key)`, which sends the key to a `Calc` object and updates `screen.text = pretty(calc.current)`. `±` flips the sign and `%` divides the current number by 100.

tests.label: The keypad drives the calculator

missions.finale: Because the logic lives in `Calc`, you could reuse it in a web page or a command-line tool without changing a line. Next challenges: memory buttons (M+, MR), or a history list.

missions.title: Capstone: Habit Forge
missions.tagline: A complete habit-tracking app with streaks, a 4-week heatmap, stats and saved data.
missions.intro: Your capstone pulls everything together: classes, dates, sets, files, JSON, testing and a real interface. **Habit Forge** lets you add habits, tick them off each day, and see streaks and a heatmap of the last four weeks. It saves everything, so it's still there tomorrow. Build it slice by slice, and every slice is tested before you move on.

steps.title: The data model
steps.text:
Write `class Habit(name)` with a `done` set of `date` objects (empty to start) and these methods:
- `toggle(day)`: mark the day done, or un-mark it if it was already done
- `is_done(day)`: True if that day is done

tests.exec:
h = Habit("Read")
assert h.done == set() and not h.is_done(TODAY)
h.toggle(TODAY)
assert h.is_done(TODAY), "toggle marks a day done"
h.toggle(TODAY)
assert not h.is_done(TODAY), "toggling again un-marks it"
tests.label: Ticking and un-ticking days

steps.title: Streaks and stats
steps.text:
Write three functions that take a `Habit`:
- `current_streak(h, today)`: days in a row ending today (or ending yesterday, if today isn't ticked yet)
- `best_streak(h)`: the longest run ever
- `rate(h, today, days=7)`: the fraction of the last `days` days (including today) that are done, as a whole percent (`round(... * 100)`)

tests.exec:
h = Habit("Run")
for back in (0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9):
    h.toggle(TODAY - timedelta(days=back))
assert current_streak(h, TODAY) == 3, f"Current streak should be 3, got {current_streak(h, TODAY)}"
assert best_streak(h) == 5, f"Best streak should be 5 (days 5 to 9 ago), got {best_streak(h)}"
assert rate(h, TODAY) == 71, f"5 of the last 7 days is 71%, got {rate(h, TODAY)}"
h.toggle(TODAY)
assert current_streak(h, TODAY) == 2, "An unticked today doesn't break the streak yet"
assert current_streak(Habit("x"), TODAY) == 0 and best_streak(Habit("x")) == 0
tests.label: Streaks and weekly rate

steps.title: Save and load
steps.text:
JSON can't store sets or dates, so convert:
- `save_habits(habits, path)`: write a list of `{"name": ..., "done": [sorted ISO date strings]}` (`day.isoformat()` gives `"2026-10-09"`)
- `load_habits(path)`: rebuild the `Habit` objects (`date.fromisoformat(text)`), or return `[]` if the file doesn't exist

tests.exec:
a, b = Habit("Read"), Habit("Stretch")
a.toggle(TODAY); a.toggle(TODAY - timedelta(days=3))
save_habits([a, b], "check.json")
with open("check.json") as f:
    raw = json.load(f)
assert raw[0] == {"name": "Read", "done": ["2026-10-06", "2026-10-09"]}, f"Saved format: {raw[0]}"
back = load_habits("check.json")
assert [h.name for h in back] == ["Read", "Stretch"] and back[0].done == a.done, "Loading gives back the same habits"
assert load_habits("nope.json") == []
tests.label: Habits survive a save and load

steps.title: The heatmap
steps.text:
Write `heatmap(h, today, weeks=4)`: a text grid of the last `weeks × 7` days, oldest first, one week per line. Each day is `■` if done or `·` if not, separated by spaces. The last character is today.
Then `summary(h, today)`: one line like `🔥 3 day streak · best 5 · 71% this week`.

tests.exec:
h = Habit("Code")
for back in (0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 27):
    h.toggle(TODAY - timedelta(days=back))
got = heatmap(h, TODAY)
want = "■ · · · · · ·\n· · · · · · ·\n· · · · ■ ■ ■\n■ ■ · · ■ ■ ■"
assert got == want, "Heatmap rows should be:\n" + want + "\n\nGot:\n" + got
assert summary(h, TODAY) == "🔥 3 day streak · best 5 · 71% this week", summary(h, TODAY)
tests.label: Heatmap and summary

steps.title: The app
steps.text:
Put a screen on it:
- load habits from `SAVE_FILE`; if there are none, start with `Read 20 minutes`, `Move your body` and `Code something`
- a title label, then an `input` and an **Add** button to create a new habit (ignore blank names and duplicates)
- a `list` of habits, each shown as `✅ Name` or `⬜ Name` for today. Clicking one toggles today and saves
- below it, the selected habit's name, `summary` and `heatmap` in labels (the heatmap label at size 22 with `mono=True`, so the squares line up)

Every change calls `save_habits` and `refresh()`, which updates every label and the list.
steps.stub:
habits = load_habits(SAVE_FILE)
app = App("Habit Forge")
app.label("Habit Forge", size=28)
steps.solution:
habits = load_habits(SAVE_FILE) or [Habit(n) for n in ("Read 20 minutes", "Move your body", "Code something")]
selected = habits[0].name

app = App("Habit Forge")
app.label("Habit Forge", size=28)
app.label(TODAY.strftime("%A, %B %d"), size=15, color="#a99fc6")
new_name = app.input("New habit, like Drink water")

def find(name):
    return next((h for h in habits if h.name == name), None)

def add():
    global selected
    name = new_name.value.strip()
    if name and not find(name):
        habits.append(Habit(name))
        selected = name
    new_name.value = ""
    changed()

add_btn = app.button("Add", add, color="#ff7a3d")
app.row([new_name, add_btn])
habit_list = app.list([])
title = app.label("", size=20)
stats = app.label("", size=16, color="#ffc94d")
grid = app.label("", size=22, mono=True)
app.label("Last 4 weeks · today is bottom right", size=13, color="#a99fc6")

def tick(item):
    global selected
    name = item[2:]
    h = find(name)
    if h:
        h.toggle(TODAY)
        selected = name
    changed()

habit_list.handler = tick

def refresh():
    habit_list.items = [("✅ " if h.is_done(TODAY) else "⬜ ") + h.name for h in habits]
    h = find(selected) or habits[0]
    title.text = h.name
    stats.text = summary(h, TODAY)
    grid.text = heatmap(h, TODAY)

def changed():
    save_habits(habits, SAVE_FILE)
    refresh()

refresh()
app.run()

tests.exec:
tick("⬜ Read 20 minutes") if "⬜ Read 20 minutes" in habit_list.items else None
assert any(i.endswith("Read 20 minutes") for i in habit_list.items), "The starter habits appear in the list"
before = len(habits)
new_name.value = "Drink water"
add()
new_name.value = "Drink water"
add()
new_name.value = "   "
add()
assert len(habits) == before + 1, "Add a new habit once; ignore blanks and duplicates"
tick("⬜ Drink water")
assert "✅ Drink water" in habit_list.items and title.text == "Drink water", "Clicking a habit ticks today and selects it"
assert stats.text.startswith("🔥 1 day streak"), stats.text
assert grid.text.endswith("■"), "The heatmap shows today as done"
assert any(h["name"] == "Drink water" for h in json.load(open(SAVE_FILE))), "Changes are saved to the file"
tick("✅ Drink water")
assert "⬜ Drink water" in habit_list.items, "Clicking again un-ticks"
tests.label: Add, tick, untick and save

missions.finale: You designed and built a complete app: data model, logic, tests, saving and an interface. That's the whole job. Ideas to make it yours: weekly goals ("3 times a week"), a "best day of the week" stat, colors per habit, or a CSV export. Then rebuild it on your laptop with a real GUI or a web page, and put it on GitHub.

missions.title: Caesar Cipher Toolkit
missions.tagline: Encrypt messages, decrypt them, and crack a cipher you don't have the key for.
missions.intro: Julius Caesar shifted every letter in his messages by 3. You'll build an encoder, a decoder, and a code-breaker that finds the key by itself.
missions.stdin:
Meet at the Old Bridge at Dawn!
7

steps.title: Encode a message
steps.text: Build `secret`: the message with every letter shifted forward by `shift`. Keep upper case upper and lower case lower, and leave everything else (spaces, punctuation) unchanged. Then print it.

tests.assert: secret == 'Tlla ha aol Vsk Iypknl ha Khdu!'
tests.label: Shift 7 encodes correctly
tests.msg: With shift 7 the message should become: Tlla ha aol Vsk Iypknl ha Khdu!

hints: Uppercase letters have codes 65–90, lowercase 97–122.

steps.title: Decode it back
steps.text: Decoding is just shifting the other way. Build `plain` by shifting every letter in `secret` back by `shift`, then print it. It should match the original message.

tests.label: Decoding gives back the original
tests.msg: plain should equal the original message.

steps.title: Crack it
steps.text: You intercepted `Wkh sdvvzrug lv vzrugilvk` but don't know the shift. Try all 25 shifts. For each, decode the text, and if the result contains the word `the`, print the shift and the decoded text like `3: the password is swordfish`.

tests.stdout:
Hi
1
Ij
Hi
3: The password is swordfish

missions.finale: Your code-breaker just did frequency-free brute force: trying every key. Real ciphers have far too many keys for that, which is exactly why they're safe.

steps.title: Load and clean
steps.text:
Write `load(path)`: read the CSV, turn `endTime` into real dates with `pd.to_datetime`, and add:
- `minutes` = msPlayed ÷ 60,000
- `skipped` = True when a track played less than 30 seconds
- `hour` = the hour of `endTime`
Return the DataFrame.
steps.solution:
def load(path):
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    df["endTime"] = pd.to_datetime(df["endTime"])
    df["minutes"] = df["msPlayed"] / 60000
    df["skipped"] = df["msPlayed"] < 30000
    df["hour"] = df["endTime"].dt.hour
    return df

steps.title: Top artists, for real
steps.text: Play counts lie: a 5-second skip counts as a play. Write `top_artists(df, n)` that returns the n artists with the most **minutes** listened (not counting skips) as a dictionary `{artist: minutes}`, minutes rounded to 1, biggest first.

steps.title: Listening habits
steps.text:
Write:
- `by_hour(df)`: minutes listened in each hour that appears, as a dictionary sorted by hour, rounded to 1
- `skip_rate(df)`: the share of plays that were skipped, as a whole-number percent
- `most_skipped(df)`: the artist with the most skips

tests.label: The morning commute is prime time

steps.title: The dashboard
steps.text:
Print a short report and draw two charts: a bar chart of your top 5 artists by minutes, and a line chart of minutes by hour.
```
Listening time: 1h 58m
Skip rate: 27% (most skipped: Bad Bunny)
Top artist: Daft Punk
```
Total time counts every play, skips included.
steps.solution:
df = load("history.csv")
total = int(df["minutes"].sum())
print(f"Listening time: {total // 60}h {total % 60}m")

missions.title: The Interview Gauntlet
missions.tagline: Five classic interview problems, tested at scale with hidden cases.
missions.intro: This is what technical interviews look like: a clear problem, edge cases you have to think of yourself, and a time limit that brute force won't beat. Each step is one problem. Hidden tests include big inputs.

steps.title: Top K frequent
steps.text: Write `top_k(nums, k)`: the k most frequent numbers, most frequent first (ties broken by the smaller number first).

steps.title: Merge intervals
steps.text: Write `merge(intervals)`: merge all overlapping `[start, end]` intervals and return them sorted. Touching intervals (`[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]`) merge too.

steps.title: Count the islands
steps.text: Write `islands(grid)`: the grid is a list of strings of `1` (land) and `0` (water). Count islands (land connected up/down/left/right). Use BFS with a deque so big grids don't hit the recursion limit.

steps.title: Longest common subsequence
steps.text: Write `lcs(a, b)`: the length of the longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order (not necessarily together). `lcs("abcde", "ace")` is 3. Use dynamic programming.

steps.title: LRU cache
steps.text: Design `LRUCache(capacity)` with `get(key)` (return the value or -1) and `put(key, value)`. When it's full, putting a new key evicts the **least recently used** one. Both operations should be O(1): `OrderedDict` with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` makes that easy.

tests.exec:
c = LRUCache(2)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
assert c.get(1) == 1
c.put(3, 3)
assert c.get(2) == -1, "2 was least recently used, so it's evicted"
c.put(4, 4)
assert c.get(1) == -1 and c.get(3) == 3 and c.get(4) == 4
tests.label: Evicts the least recently used key

tests.exec:
c = LRUCache(1000)
for i in range(200000):
    c.put(i, i)
    c.get(i - 500)
assert c.get(199999) == 199999
tests.label: 400,000 operations stay fast

missions.finale: Hash maps, sorting, BFS, dynamic programming and a data structure design: you just covered the five most common interview categories. Keep the streak going in the Dojo's harder puzzles.

missions.title: Loan Calculator

Then write `balance_after(amount, annual_rate, years, months)`: simulate month by month (add one month of interest, subtract the payment) and return the remaining balance after `months` payments, rounded to 2 decimals.

steps.text: Write `cheapest(amount, annual_rate, options)` where options is a range or list of loan lengths in years. Return the number of years with the lowest total interest. (Hint: shorter loans cost less interest, but check it with code.)

missions.title: Server Log Detective
missions.tagline: Parse a web server's logs to find errors, busy hours and a suspicious visitor.
missions.intro: Every website writes a log line for each request. When something breaks, engineers dig through these logs. You'll use regex, datetime and Counter to turn thousands of lines into answers.

steps.title: Parse each line
steps.text:
`LINE` is a regex with 6 groups: IP, timestamp, method, path, status, bytes.
Write `parse(line)` that returns a dictionary with keys `ip`, `time` (a `datetime`, the format is `%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S`), `method`, `path`, `status` (int) and `bytes` (int), or None if the line doesn't match.
Then `load(path)` returns the list of parsed lines, skipping None.

steps.title: The numbers

Write three functions:
- `error_rate(rows)`: share of requests with status ≥ 400, rounded to 2
- `busiest_hour(rows)`: the hour (0–23) with the most requests
- `top_paths(rows, n)`: the n most requested paths as Counter's `most_common` list

steps.title: Catch the intruder
steps.text:
Someone tried to brute-force the login. Write `suspicious_ips(rows, limit=3)` that returns a sorted list of IPs with **more than** `limit` failed logins (POST to `/login` with status 401).
Also write `broken_paths(rows)`: the sorted set of paths that returned a 5xx server error.

```

Error rate: 44%
Busiest hour: 10:00
Top paths: /login (5), /shop (3), /index.html (2)
```

missions.title: Maze Solver
missions.tagline: A recursive explorer that finds its way out of any maze.
missions.intro: Your solver will stand at S, try a direction, and if it hits a dead end, back up and try another. That "back up" is what recursion gives you for free. It's called **backtracking**.

steps.title: Find S and E
steps.text: Write `find(maze, ch)` that returns `(row, col)` of the first cell containing `ch`, or None.

steps.title: Where can I step?
steps.text: Write `neighbours(maze, cell)` that returns the cells up, down, left and right of `cell` (in that order) that are inside the maze and not walls (`#`).

steps.title: Solve it recursively
steps.text:
Write `solve(maze, cell, goal, visited)`. It returns a path (a list of cells from `cell` to `goal`), or None if there's no way through from here.
- If `cell == goal`, the path is just `[cell]`.
- Add `cell` to `visited`. For each neighbour not yet visited, try `solve` from there. If it finds a path, return `[cell] + path`.
- If no neighbour works, return None (dead end: backtrack).
steps.stub:
def solve(maze, cell, goal, visited):
    return None

tests.exec:
path = solve(MAZE, find(MAZE, "S"), find(MAZE, "E"), set())
assert path is not None, "solve() should find a path out of this maze"
assert path[0] == (1, 1) and path[-1] == (7, 9), "The path must go from S to E"
for a, b in zip(path, path[1:]):
    assert abs(a[0] - b[0]) + abs(a[1] - b[1]) == 1, "Each step moves exactly one cell"
    assert MAZE[b[0]][b[1]] != "#", "The path can't go through walls"
tests.label: Finds a valid path from S to E
Returns None when there's no way out

steps.title: Draw the route
steps.text: Print the maze with the path drawn in `*` (keep S and E as they are), then print `Path length: N` where N is the number of steps (cells in the path minus one).
steps.solution:
path = solve(MAZE, find(MAZE, "S"), find(MAZE, "E"), set())
grid = [list(row) for row in MAZE]
for r, c in path[1:-1]:
    grid[r][c] = "*"
for row in grid:
    print("".join(row))
print(f"Path length: {len(path) - 1}")

missions.finale: Depth-first search finds *a* way out, not always the shortest. In the Serious Coder stage you'll write breadth-first search, which always finds the shortest path. Try designing a harder maze!

missions.title: Obby Engine
missions.tagline: Build an obstacle course in Block World, then script the game behind it with events, checkpoints and a leaderboard.
missions.intro: An **obby** (obstacle course) is the classic first game people script in block-building engines: jump across platforms over lava, hit checkpoints, beat the clock. The building is the easy part. The real game is the script: what happens on every touch, where you respawn, and who tops the leaderboard. You'll write all of it in Python, the same event-driven way game scripts work.

steps.title: Build the course
steps.text:
Write `platform(x, y, z, block)` that fills a 3 × 3 square of `block` centered on `(x, y, z)`. Then `build_course()`:
- a lava lake: `fill(5, 0, 8, 29, 0, 28, "lava")` replaces the grass under the course
- every stage gets a platform: `"obsidian"` for the start, `"diamond"` for the finish, `"gold"` for checkpoint stages, and the rest alternate `"wool_blue"` (even index) and `"wool_white"` (odd)
- a `"cobble"` pillar under each platform's center, from y = 1 up to just below the platform, so you can see how high each one is
- a `"glow"` block on top of the finish platform's center, one level up
Call `build_course()` after defining it and press **Run**.

tests.assert: get(15, 4, 12) == "gold" and get(26, 7, 18) == "gold" and get(7, 2, 16) == "wool_white" and get(11, 3, 14) == "wool_blue"

tests.label: Pillars

steps.title: An event system
steps.text:
Game engines tell your script what happened through events. Write `class Signal` with `connect(fn)` and `fire(*args)` (call every connected function with those arguments, in order).
Then create one signal: `touched = Signal()`. Every time a player lands on something, the game will call `touched.fire(player, stage_index)`.

tests.exec:
s = Signal()
seen = []
s.connect(lambda a, b: seen.append(("first", a, b)))
s.connect(lambda a, b: seen.append(("second", a, b)))
s.fire("kai", 3)
assert seen == [("first", "kai", 3), ("second", "kai", 3)], f"Every handler runs, in order: {seen}"
tests.label: Handlers run in order

steps.title: Players and checkpoints
steps.text:
Write `class Player(name)` with `stage = 0`, `checkpoint = 0`, `deaths = 0` and `finished = False`.
Then write `on_touch(player, stage)` and connect it to `touched`:
- `stage` of `-1` means they fell in the lava: add a death and send them back to their `checkpoint`
- otherwise move them to that stage; if it's a checkpoint stage, save it as their `checkpoint`
- reaching the last stage sets `finished = True`

    touched.fire(p, s)
assert p.stage == 4 and p.checkpoint == 3, "Landing on stage 3 saves it as a checkpoint"
touched.fire(p, -1)
assert p.stage == 3 and p.deaths == 1, "Lava sends you back to your last checkpoint"
touched.fire(p, len(STAGES) - 1)
assert p.finished, "Reaching the last stage finishes the course"
tests.label: Lava, checkpoints and the finish (through the touched event)

tests.exec:
p = Player("max")
touched.fire(p, 1)
touched.fire(p, -1)
assert p.stage == 0 and p.deaths == 1, "Without a checkpoint you go back to the start"
tests.label: No checkpoint means back to the start

steps.text:
Simulate a race. Write `run_course(player, skill, max_jumps=300)`: each jump takes 1.5 seconds. With chance `skill` (use `random.random() < skill`) the jump lands, and you fire `touched` with the next stage; otherwise fire `touched` with `-1`. Stop when they finish or run out of jumps. Return the time in seconds, or `None` if they never finished.
Then `leaderboard(results)`: given a list of `(name, time, deaths)`, drop anyone whose time is `None` and sort by time, then fewest deaths. Finally race four players, print the leaderboard as `1. Name  21.0s  (2 deaths)`, and put a `"gold"` trophy block above the finish for the winner.

tests.exec:

assert run_course(p, 1.0) == 1.5 * (len(STAGES) - 1), "A perfect player needs one 1.5 s jump per stage"
assert p.finished and p.deaths == 0

tests.label: Running the course

missions.title: Downloads Folder Cleaner
missions.tagline: Sort a messy folder in one run, safely, with an Excel report at the end.
missions.intro: Everyone's Downloads folder is a mess. You'll build a cleaner that sorts files into folders by type, never overwrites anything, can do a dry run first, and writes an Excel report of what it did.

steps.title: Classify a file
steps.text: Write `category(path)` that returns the category name for a `Path` from `CATEGORIES`, matching the extension case-insensitively, or `"Other"`.

steps.title: Plan the moves (dry run)
steps.text: Write `plan(folder)` that returns a sorted list of `(source, destination)` Path pairs for every **file** directly inside the folder (not in subfolders), where the destination is `folder / category / name`. Don't move anything yet.

tests.call: [str(d) for s, d in plan("Downloads") if s.name == "song.mp3"]

steps.title: Move safely
steps.text:
Write `safe_destination(dest)`: if `dest` already exists, add ` (1)`, ` (2)`... before the extension until the name is free (`notes.txt` becomes `notes (1).txt`).
Then `organize(folder)` carries out the plan: create category folders as needed, move each file to its safe destination, and return a list of `(category, name, size_in_bytes)` for the report.
steps.solution:
def safe_destination(dest):
    n = 1
    candidate = dest
    while candidate.exists():
        candidate = dest.with_name(f"{dest.stem} ({n}){dest.suffix}")
        n += 1
    return candidate

def organize(folder):
    done = []
    for src, dest in plan(folder):
        dest.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        final = safe_destination(dest)
        size = src.stat().st_size
        src.rename(final)
        done.append((dest.parent.name, final.name, size))
    return done

tests.exec:
moved = organize("Downloads")
assert len(moved) == 11, f"All 11 loose files should move, moved {len(moved)}"
left = [p.name for p in Path("Downloads").iterdir() if p.is_file()]
assert left == [], f"No loose files should remain, found {left}"
assert (Path("Downloads") / "Documents" / "notes.txt").exists()
assert (Path("Downloads") / "Images" / "notes.txt").read_text() == "already here", "Never overwrite an existing file"
assert (Path("Downloads") / "Video" / "clip.mov").exists()
tests.label: Every file moves, nothing is overwritten

steps.title: The Excel report
steps.text: Run the cleaner and write `cleanup_report.xlsx` with a bold header `Category, Files, Size (KB)` and one row per category (sorted by name), sizes in KB rounded to 2. Then print `Moved 11 files into 5 folders`.
steps.solution:
moved = organize("Downloads")
summary = {}
for cat, name, size in moved:
    files, total = summary.get(cat, (0, 0))
    summary[cat] = (files + 1, total + size)
wb = Workbook()
ws = wb.active
ws.title = "Cleanup"
ws.append(["Category", "Files", "Size (KB)"])
for cell in ws[1]:
    cell.font = Font(bold=True)
for cat in sorted(summary):
    files, size = summary[cat]
    ws.append([cat, files, round(size / 1024, 2)])
wb.save("cleanup_report.xlsx")
print(f"Moved {len(moved)} files into {len(summary)} folders")

tests.exec:
from openpyxl import load_workbook
rows = list(load_workbook("cleanup_report.xlsx").active.iter_rows(values_only=True))
assert rows[0] == ("Category", "Files", "Size (KB)")
assert [r[0] for r in rows[1:]] == ["Archives", "Audio", "Documents", "Images", "Video"], f"Categories: {[r[0] for r in rows[1:]]}"
