missions.finale: Export this as a .py file, point it at your real Downloads folder (run with a dry run first!), and schedule it weekly. That's an hour a month saved, forever.

missions.title: Ship a Command-Line Tool
missions.tagline: Build "jot", a real notes app for the terminal, with subcommands, saved data and tests.
missions.intro: Developers live in the terminal, and the tools they love are small programs like `git` and `pip`. You'll build **jot**: `jot add "Call the dentist" --tag health`, `jot list`, `jot search dentist`, `jot done 3`. It saves to a JSON file, returns proper exit codes, and comes with its own tests. Copy it to your laptop afterwards and it works for real.

steps.title: Save and load
steps.text:
Write `load_notes(path)`: return the list stored in the JSON file, or `[]` if the file doesn't exist yet.
Write `save_notes(path, notes)`: write the list to the file with `json.dump(..., indent=2)` so it stays readable.

tests.exec:
save_notes("check.json", [{"id": 1, "text": "hi"}])
assert load_notes("check.json") == [{"id": 1, "text": "hi"}], "What you save should load back the same"
assert load_notes("does-not-exist.json") == [], "A missing file means no notes yet"
tests.label: Notes survive a save and load

steps.title: The core logic
steps.text:
Keep logic separate from the command line so it's easy to test:
- `add_note(notes, text, tags=())`: append and return a note `{"id", "text", "tags", "done", "date"}`. The id is one more than the biggest existing id (1 for the first). Tags are sorted with duplicates removed. `done` starts False; `date` is `TODAY`.
- `find(notes, word)`: notes whose text contains `word`, ignoring case.
- `complete(notes, note_id)`: mark that note done and return True, or return False if there's no such id.

tests.exec:
notes = []
a = add_note(notes, "Buy milk", ["food", "errand", "food"])
b = add_note(notes, "Call Sam")
assert a == {"id": 1, "text": "Buy milk", "tags": ["errand", "food"], "done": False, "date": TODAY}, f"First note looks wrong: {a}"
assert b["id"] == 2 and len(notes) == 2, "Ids count up, and notes are added to the list"
notes.pop(0)
assert add_note(notes, "x")["id"] == 3, "Ids never repeat, even after deleting a note"
tests.label: Adding notes

tests.call: [n["id"] for n in find([{"id": 1, "text": "Buy MILK"}, {"id": 2, "text": "Call Sam"}], "milk")]
tests.label: Search ignores case

tests.exec:
notes = [{"id": 4, "text": "a", "done": False}]
assert complete(notes, 4) is True and notes[0]["done"], "Completing a real note marks it done"
assert complete(notes, 99) is False, "An unknown id returns False"
tests.label: Completing notes

steps.title: The command line
steps.text:
Write `build_parser()` with argparse **subcommands** (`p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)`), like git's:
- `add TEXT` with a repeatable `--tag` (`action="append", default=[]`)
- `list` with an `--all` flag (`action="store_true"`) to include finished notes
- `search WORD`
- `done ID` where ID is an int
Give the parser `prog="jot"` and a description so `--help` looks professional.
steps.solution:
def build_parser():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="jot", description="Tiny notes for your terminal.")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    add = sub.add_parser("add", help="add a note")
    add.add_argument("text")
    add.add_argument("--tag", action="append", default=[], help="tag the note (repeatable)")
    ls = sub.add_parser("list", help="show open notes")
    ls.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="include finished notes")
    search = sub.add_parser("search", help="find notes containing a word")
    search.add_argument("word")
    done = sub.add_parser("done", help="mark a note finished")
    done.add_argument("id", type=int)
    return p

tests.label: Every subcommand parses

steps.title: Wire it together
steps.text:
Write `main(argv, path=NOTES_FILE)`: parse `argv`, load the notes, run the command, save if anything changed, and **return an exit code**:
- `add`: print `Added #<id>`, return 0
- `list`: print each open note (all notes with `--all`) using `fmt(note)`, or `Nothing to do!`; return 0
- `search`: print matches with `fmt`, or `No matches`; return 0 if found, 1 if not
- `done`: print `Done #<id>` and return 0, or print `No note #<id>` to `sys.stderr` and return 1

`fmt(note)` gives one line: `✔` or `•`, the id right-aligned in 3 spaces, two spaces, the text, then `  #tag1 #tag2` if it has tags.

tests.exec:
import io, contextlib
if os.path.exists("t.json"):
    os.remove("t.json")
def run(*words):
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf), contextlib.redirect_stderr(buf):
        code = main(list(words), "t.json")
    return code, buf.getvalue().strip()
assert run("add", "Water plants", "--tag", "home") == (0, "Added #1")
assert run("add", "Email Ana") == (0, "Added #2")
assert run("done", "1") == (0, "Done #1")
assert run("list") == (0, "•   2  Email Ana"), f"list shows open notes only: {run('list')}"
code, out = run("list", "--all")
assert out.count("\n") == 1 and "✔   1  Water plants  #home" in out, "list --all includes finished notes"
assert run("search", "ANA") == (0, "•   2  Email Ana")
assert run("search", "zebra") == (1, "No matches"), "No matches returns exit code 1"
assert run("done", "9") == (1, "No note #9"), "Unknown ids return exit code 1"
assert len(load_notes("t.json")) == 2, "Changes are saved to the file"
tests.label: Every command works end to end

steps.title: Test it like a pro
steps.text:
Write at least three pytest-style test functions (names starting with `test_`) for jot. Each should use its own file (like `"test_a.json"`), deleting it first if it exists, and call `main([...], path)` and/or the core functions. Ideas: ids keep counting after `done`; `search` is case-insensitive; `done` with a bad id returns 1.
The check runs every `test_` function you write. On your laptop, `pytest` would find and run them the same way.
steps.solution:
def fresh(path):
    if os.path.exists(path):
        os.remove(path)
    return path

def test_ids_keep_counting():
    path = fresh("test_ids.json")
    main(["add", "one"], path)
    main(["add", "two"], path)
    main(["done", "1"], path)
    main(["add", "three"], path)
    assert [n["id"] for n in load_notes(path)] == [1, 2, 3]

def test_search_ignores_case():
    path = fresh("test_search.json")
    main(["add", "Buy Oat Milk"], path)
    assert main(["search", "oat"], path) == 0
    assert main(["search", "OAT"], path) == 0

def test_bad_id_fails():
    path = fresh("test_bad.json")
    assert main(["done", "5"], path) == 1

tests.label: At least 3 real tests, all passing

missions.finale: You shipped a real tool: subcommands, saved data, exit codes and tests. To use it for real, save the file as `jot.py` on your laptop, then run `python3 jot.py add "something"`. Next: add `jot delete`, due dates, or color with the `rich` package, then put it on GitHub.

missions.title: Sorting Visualizer
missions.tagline: Watch bubble, selection and insertion sort race, bar by bar.
missions.intro: Sorting algorithms are easier to understand when you can watch them. You'll make each algorithm **record a snapshot** of the list every time it swaps or moves something, then play the snapshots back like a flip book.
missions.scaffold:
from forge import *
import random

WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 500
TITLE = "Sorting Visualizer"
CONTROLS = ["space", "left", "right"]
N = 36

{{bubble}}

{{selection}}

{{insertion}}

ALGORITHMS = [("Bubble sort", bubble_frames), ("Selection sort", selection_frames), ("Insertion sort", insertion_frames)]
algo = 0
frames = []
frame = 0.0
speed = 30


def new_run():
    global frames, frame
    data = list(range(1, N + 1))
    random.shuffle(data)
    frames = ALGORITHMS[algo][1](data)
    if not frames:
        frames = [(data, ())]
    frame = 0.0

new_run()

{{draw}}


def update(dt):
    global frame, algo, speed
    if keyboard.pressed("space"):
        algo = (algo + 1) % len(ALGORITHMS)
        new_run()
    if keyboard.pressed("right"):
        speed = min(speed * 2, 960)
    if keyboard.pressed("left"):
        speed = max(speed / 2, 2)
    before = int(frame)
    frame = min(frame + speed * dt, len(frames) - 1)
    if int(frame) != before and int(frame) % 3 == 0:
        sound.play("click")

steps.title: Record bubble sort
steps.text: Write `bubble_frames(data)`. Sort a **copy** of data with bubble sort, and every time you swap two items, append a frame: `(a[:], (i, i + 1))` (a copy of the list, plus the two positions that just swapped). Return the list of frames.

tests.label: The last frame is fully sorted

steps.title: Draw the bars
steps.text:
Write `draw()`. Show the current frame `frames[int(frame)]`: each value `v` is a bar whose height is proportional to v (the tallest, N, should be about 400 pixels). Bars sit on the bottom of the screen, side by side across the width.
Color the two highlighted positions differently, and show the algorithm name, the step number and the total steps at the top.
steps.solution:
def draw():
    screen.clear("#120f22")
    values, hot = frames[int(frame)]
    bar_w = WIDTH / len(values)
    for i, v in enumerate(values):
        h = v / N * 400
        color = "#ff7a3d" if i in hot else "#6fd3ff"
        if int(frame) == len(frames) - 1:
            color = "#4be38f"
        screen.rect(i * bar_w + 2, HEIGHT - h - 10, bar_w - 4, h, color, radius=3)
    name = ALGORITHMS[algo][0]
    screen.text(f"{name}   step {int(frame) + 1} / {len(frames)}", 20, 18, 24, "white")
    screen.text("space: next algorithm   ← →: speed", 20, 50, 16, "#a99fc6")

tests.exec:
import forge._game as g
g._cmds.clear()
draw()
bars = [c for c in g._cmds if c[0] == "r"]
assert len(bars) >= N, f"Draw one bar per value ({N} bars), found {len(bars)}"
tallest = max(c[4] for c in bars)
assert 300 <= tallest <= 480, f"The tallest bar should be about 400 px high, got {tallest}"
tests.label: One bar per value, scaled to the screen

steps.title: Record selection sort
steps.text:
Write `selection_frames(data)` the same way: after each swap of the smallest remaining item into place, append `(a[:], (i, smallest))`. Only record a frame when `i != smallest`.
Press **space** while the game runs to switch algorithms and compare.

steps.title: Record insertion sort
steps.text:
Write `insertion_frames(data)`. Each time an item shifts one place to the right while you slide the current card into position, append `(a[:], (j, j + 1))`, recorded **after** the shift.
Then compare all three: which one needs the fewest frames on random data?
steps.solution:
def insertion_frames(data):
    a = data[:]
    frames = []
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        x = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > x:
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            a[j] = x
            frames.append((a[:], (j, j + 1)))
            j -= 1
    return frames

missions.finale: Selection sort makes the fewest swaps but always does n² comparisons. Bubble and insertion sort make the same number of moves, but insertion sort stops early on nearly-sorted data. Now you've seen it, not just read it.

missions.title: Study Buddy Bot
missions.tagline: A chatbot that answers from your own notes, the idea behind real AI search.
missions.intro: Chatbots that answer questions about *your* documents work in two parts: **retrieve** the most relevant notes, then **answer** using them. You'll build both, with a confidence threshold so it says "I don't know" instead of making things up.
missions.stdin:
what does a for loop do
how do I install packages
who won the world cup
quit

steps.title: Clean the words
steps.text: Write `tokens(text)`: lowercase the text, pull out words with `re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", ...)`, drop words in `STOP`, and drop a trailing `s` from words longer than 3 letters (so "loops" and "loop" match). Return the list.

tests.call: tokens("What does a for loop do")

steps.title: Vectors and similarity
steps.text: Write `vector(words)`: a dictionary counting each word. Then `similarity(a, b)`: cosine similarity between two such dictionaries (dot product over shared words ÷ product of their lengths), 0 if either is empty.

steps.title: Retrieve and answer
steps.text: Write `answer(question, threshold=0.2)`: score every note against the question, pick the best one, and return it if its score is at least `threshold`. Otherwise return `"I don't know that one yet."`. Never guess.
steps.stub:
def answer(question, threshold=0.2):
    return "I don't know that one yet."
steps.solution:
def answer(question, threshold=0.2):
    q = vector(tokens(question))
    scored = [(similarity(q, vector(tokens(n))), n) for n in NOTES]
    best_score, best_note = max(scored)
    return best_note if best_score >= threshold else "I don't know that one yet."

steps.title: The chat loop
steps.text: Read questions until `quit` and print `Bot: <answer>` for each.

tests.stdin:
what does a for loop do
how do I install packages
who won the world cup
quit
tests.stdout:
what does a for loop do
Bot: A for loop repeats a block of code once for every item in a sequence, like a list or a range.
how do I install packages
Bot: Install packages with pip, for example pip install requests, ideally inside a virtual environment.
who won the world cup
Bot: I don't know that one yet.
quit

missions.finale: Swap NOTES for your own class notes and you have a study tool. Connect `answer()` to a real AI model, passing the top 3 notes as context, and you've built RAG, the technique behind most "chat with your documents" products.

missions.title: Build Your Own Test Framework
missions.tagline: Recreate the core of pytest with decorators, a context manager and closures.
missions.intro: pytest is one of the most-used Python tools in the world, and its core ideas fit on one screen. You'll build **testkit**: an `@test` decorator that registers tests, a `raises()` context manager, a runner that reports passes and failures, and `@parametrize` to run one test with many inputs. At the bottom, real tests use your framework. Watch them light up as you build each piece.

steps.title: Register tests
steps.text: Write a decorator `test(fn)` that appends `(fn.__name__, fn)` to `TESTS` and returns `fn` **unchanged**, so the function still works normally. That's all `@test` needs to do: the runner finds tests through the list.

tests.exec:
before = len(TESTS)
@test
def test_sample():
    return 42
assert len(TESTS) == before + 1 and TESTS[-1] == ("test_sample", test_sample), "@test should add (name, function) to TESTS"
assert test_sample() == 42, "The decorated function still works"
del TESTS[-1]
tests.label: @test registers the function
The tests at the bottom are registered in order

steps.title: Expect an error
steps.text:
Write a class `raises(expected)`, used as `with raises(ZeroDivisionError):`.
- `__enter__` returns `self`
- `__exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb)`:
  - no exception happened (`exc_type is None`): raise `AssertionError(f"Expected {expected.__name__}, but nothing was raised")`
  - the exception is `expected` or a subclass (`issubclass`): save it as `self.value` and return `True`, which tells Python "handled, don't re-raise"
  - any other exception: return `False` so it keeps going

tests.exec:
with raises(ZeroDivisionError) as r:
    1 / 0
assert isinstance(r.value, ZeroDivisionError), "The caught exception is saved as .value"
with raises(LookupError):
    {}["missing"]
tests.label: Catches the expected error (and subclasses)
Fails when nothing is raised
Lets other errors through

steps.title: The runner
steps.text:
Write `run_tests(tests=None)` (use `TESTS` when none are given). Call each test function:
- it returns normally: print `✓ name`
- `AssertionError`: print `✗ name: message` (or `✗ name: assertion failed` if the message is empty)
- any other exception: print `✗ name: TypeName: message` (it crashed rather than failed)
Finish with `N passed, M failed` and return `(passed, failed)`.

tests.exec:
import io, contextlib
def ok(): pass
def bad(): assert 1 == 2, "math is broken"
def blank(): assert False
def crash(): {}["k"]
buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
    result = run_tests([("ok", ok), ("bad", bad), ("blank", blank), ("crash", crash)])
want = "✓ ok\n✗ bad: math is broken\n✗ blank: assertion failed\n✗ crash: KeyError: 'k'\n1 passed, 3 failed"
got = buf.getvalue().strip()
assert got == want, "Expected:\n" + want + "\n\nGot:\n" + got
assert result == (1, 3), f"Return (passed, failed), got {result}"
tests.label: Reports passes, failures and crashes

steps.title: One test, many inputs
steps.text:
Write `parametrize(cases)`, a decorator **factory**: it returns a decorator. For each tuple in `cases`, register a test named `f"{fn.__name__}[{i}]"` (i counts from 0) that calls `fn(*case)`.
Watch out for the late-binding trap from this unit's challenge: each registered test must remember **its own** case. A default argument (`lambda case=case: fn(*case)`) or a helper function fixes it.

tests.call: [name for name, fn in TESTS if name.startswith('test_add')]
tests.label: One test per case
Each test keeps its own case

tests.stdout:
✓ test_slugify_basic
✓ test_slugify_spaces
✓ test_divide_by_zero
✗ test_known_bug: punctuation isn't removed yet
✓ test_add[0]
✓ test_add[1]
✓ test_add[2]
6 passed, 1 failed
tests.label: The whole suite runs

missions.finale: That's the heart of pytest: decorators to register tests, a context manager for expected errors, closures for parametrized cases, and a runner. Now fix `slugify` so `test_known_bug` passes (hint: keep only letters, digits and spaces), and watch your own framework turn it green.

missions.title: Unbeatable Tic-Tac-Toe
missions.tagline: A board, a referee, and a computer opponent that never loses.
missions.intro: You'll play X, the computer plays O. You'll write the board, the referee that spots a winner, and an AI that follows a simple strategy good enough to never lose.

steps.title: Draw the board
steps.text:
Write `show(board)` that prints the board like this (each cell is X, O or a space):
```
 X | O |
---+---+---
   | X |
---+---+---
   |   | O
```
Each row is ` a | b | c `, separated by `---+---+---`.

tests.exec:
import io, contextlib
b = [["X", "O", " "], [" ", "X", " "], [" ", " ", "O"]]
buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
    show(b)
want = " X | O |   \n---+---+---\n   | X |   \n---+---+---\n   |   | O "
assert buf.getvalue().rstrip("\n") == want, "show() printed:\n" + buf.getvalue()
tests.label: The board prints in a 3 × 3 layout

steps.title: The referee
steps.text: Write `winner(board)` that returns `"X"` or `"O"` if that player has three in a row (any row, column or diagonal), `"draw"` if the board is full, otherwise None.

steps.title: The AI
steps.text:
Write `best_move(board)` that returns `(row, col)` for O using this strategy, in order:
1. If O can win right now, do it.
2. If X could win next move, block that square.
3. Take the center if it's free.
4. Take a free corner (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right order).
5. Otherwise take the first free square.
Tip: to test a move, place the mark, call `winner`, then undo it.

steps.title: Play the game
steps.text:
Now the game loop. Repeat until `winner(board)` returns something:
- read your move as a number 1–9 (1 is top-left, 9 is bottom-right). If the square is taken, print `Taken` and read again.
- place X, and stop if the game is over
- let the AI place O and print `O plays N` (N from 1 to 9)
Then `show(board)` and print `X wins!`, `O wins!` or `Draw!`.
steps.solution:
while winner(board) is None:
    n = int(input()) - 1
    r, c = divmod(n, 3)
    if board[r][c] != " ":
        print("Taken")
        continue
    board[r][c] = "X"
    if winner(board) is not None:
        break
    r, c = best_move(board)
    board[r][c] = "O"
    print(f"O plays {r * 3 + c + 1}")
show(board)
result = winner(board)
print("Draw!" if result == "draw" else f"{result} wins!")

Taken

---+---+---

---+---+---
 X | O | X
Draw!

1
O plays 5

---+---+---

missions.title: To-Do List
missions.tagline: A command-line task manager with add, done, list and stats.
missions.intro: Command-line tools are how programmers get things done. You'll build a to-do manager that reads commands like `add Buy milk`, `done 1` and `list`.
missions.stdin:
add Buy milk
add Finish Python unit
add Call mom
done 2
list
stats
quit

steps.title: Add tasks
steps.text: Write `add_task(text)`: append the text to `tasks` and `False` to `done` (the two lists stay in step, so task `i` is finished when `done[i]` is True).

tests.exec:
tasks.clear(); done.clear()
add_task("Write code")
add_task("Test it")
assert tasks == ["Write code", "Test it"], f"tasks should be ['Write code', 'Test it'], got {tasks}"
assert done == [False, False], "Each new task starts as not done"
tests.label: Tasks are added

steps.title: Mark tasks done
steps.text: Write `complete(number)`. Users count from 1, so task number 1 is index 0. Set that task's `done` entry to True and return True. If the number is out of range, return False and change nothing.

tests.exec:
tasks.clear(); done.clear()
add_task("a"); add_task("b")
assert complete(2) is True and done == [False, True], "complete(2) should mark the second task"
assert complete(5) is False and complete(0) is False, "Numbers out of range return False"
tests.label: Tasks can be completed by number

steps.title: Show the list
steps.text:
Write `show()` that prints each task as `1. [ ] Buy milk` or `2. [x] Call mom` (x when done). If there are no tasks, print `Nothing to do!`.
Write `stats()` that returns a string like `1/3 done (33%)`, with the percentage rounded down.

tests.exec:
tasks.clear(); done.clear()
add_task("a"); add_task("b"); add_task("c")
complete(2)
assert stats() == "1/3 done (33%)", f"stats() should be '1/3 done (33%)', got {stats()!r}"
tests.label: stats() reports progress

tests.exec:
import io, contextlib
tasks.clear(); done.clear()
add_task("Buy milk"); add_task("Call mom"); complete(2)
buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
    show()
assert buf.getvalue().strip() == "1. [ ] Buy milk\n2. [x] Call mom", f"show() printed:\n{buf.getvalue()}"
tests.label: show() prints numbered tasks with checkboxes

steps.title: The command loop
steps.text:
Finally, read commands until `quit`:
- `add <text>` adds a task
- `done <n>` completes task n, or prints `No task n` if it doesn't exist
- `list` calls show()
- `stats` prints stats()
- anything else prints `Unknown command`
Tip: `command.split(" ", 1)` splits into the first word and the rest.

tests.stdin:
add Buy milk
add Finish Python unit
add Call mom
done 2
list
stats
quit

add Finish Python unit
add Call mom

2. [x] Finish Python unit
3. [ ] Call mom
stats
1/3 done (33%)
quit

list
Nothing to do!
done 4
No task 4
fly
Unknown command
quit

missions.finale: That command loop is the same pattern behind real CLI tools like git. Want more? Add a `delete n` command, or save tasks to a file in Stage 3.

missions.title: Weather App
missions.tagline: A real app with live forecasts for any city on Earth.
missions.intro: You'll build a working weather app: type a city, tap Search, see the current conditions and a 3-day forecast, live from the free Open-Meteo API. Run it on your phone with an internet connection.

steps.title: Find the city
steps.text:
Write `geocode_url(city)` for `https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search` with parameters `name` = the city and `count` = 1.
Write `parse_place(data)` that returns `{"name", "country", "lat", "lon"}` from the first result, or None if there are no results.

steps.title: Read the forecast
steps.text:
Write `forecast_url(lat, lon)` for `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast` with `latitude`, `longitude`, `current` = `temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m,weather_code`, `daily` = `temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min,weather_code`, and `forecast_days` = 3.
Write `parse_forecast(data)` that returns `{"temp", "wind", "sky", "days"}` where `sky` comes from `WMO` (default `"?"`) and `days` is a list of `(date, low, high, sky)` tuples.

steps.title: Fetch it for real
steps.text:
Write `fetch_json(url)`: `requests.get(url, timeout=10)`, raise an error unless the status is 200 (`r.raise_for_status()` does that), and return `r.json()`.
Then `get_weather(city, fetch=None)` uses `fetch or fetch_json` to look up the place and its forecast, and returns `(place, forecast)`. If the city isn't found, raise `LookupError(f"Couldn't find {city}")`.
(Passing `fetch` in lets the tests use saved data instead of the internet.)

tests.label: Missing cities raise LookupError

steps.title: The app
steps.text:
Build the screen with `forge.ui`:
- `app = App("Weather")`, an input `city`, a `Search` button, and labels for the place (big), the conditions, and the 3-day forecast
- `search()` calls `get_weather(city.value, FETCH)` and fills in the labels, like `Lisbon, Portugal`, `21.4°C · Mostly clear 🌤 · wind 14.0 km/h`, and one line per day
- if anything goes wrong (no internet, unknown city), show the error message in the place label instead of crashing
`FETCH = None` means "use the real internet". Press **Run**, type a city and tap Search.
steps.solution:
FETCH = None
app = App("Weather")
city = app.input("City, like Tokyo", on_enter=lambda v: search())
app.button("Search", lambda: search(), color="#6fd3ff")
place_label = app.label("Search for a city", size=30)
now_label = app.label("", size=18)
days_label = app.label("", size=16)

def search():
    name = city.value.strip()
    if not name:
        place_label.text = "Type a city first"
        return
    try:
        place, fc = get_weather(name, FETCH)
    except Exception as e:
        place_label.text = str(e) if isinstance(e, LookupError) else "Couldn't load the weather. Check your connection."
        now_label.text = days_label.text = ""
        return
    place_label.text = f"{place['name']}, {place['country']}"
    now_label.text = f"{fc['temp']}°C · {fc['sky']} · wind {fc['wind']} km/h"
    days_label.text = "\n".join(f"{d[5:]}  {lo:.0f}–{hi:.0f}°  {sky}" for d, lo, hi, sky in fc["days"])

app.run()

tests.exec:
FETCH = fake_fetch
city.value = "Lisbon"
search()
assert place_label.text == "Lisbon, Portugal", f"The place label shows {place_label.text!r}"
assert "21.4" in now_label.text, "Show the current temperature"
assert days_label.text.count("\n") == 2, "Show 3 forecast lines"
city.value = "Atlantis"
search()
assert "Atlantis" in place_label.text, "Unknown cities show a friendly message"
FETCH = None
tests.label: Search fills in the screen and handles errors

missions.finale: That's a real app: user input, a live API, parsing, error handling and a UI. Ideas: show the hourly forecast, remember the last city, or add a °F toggle.

missions.title: Text Analyzer
missions.tagline: Word counts, top words and reading time, for any essay or article.
missions.intro: Writers, students and SEO folks all want the same stats about their text. You'll build an analyzer that works on any text, then try it on your own writing.

steps.title: Split into words
steps.text: Write `get_words(text)` that returns a list of the words in lowercase, with the punctuation `.,;:!?"'()` stripped from each word's edges. Skip anything that ends up empty.

steps.title: Count everything
steps.text: Write `count_words(words)` that returns a dictionary of word counts, and `unique_ratio(words)` that returns the share of distinct words (distinct ÷ total), rounded to 2 decimals.

steps.title: Find the top words
steps.text: Write `top_words(counts, n, ignore)` that returns the n most common words as a list of `(word, count)` pairs, skipping words in the `ignore` set. Sort by count (highest first), and alphabetically when counts tie.
steps.solution:
def top_words(counts, n, ignore):
    pairs = [(w, c) for w, c in counts.items() if w not in ignore]
    pairs.sort(key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))
    return pairs[:n]
hints: Sort with key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]). The minus sign makes bigger counts come first.

steps.title: The report
steps.text:
Print a report for `TEXT`, exactly like this. Reading time assumes 200 words per minute, rounded up to at least 1 minute.
```
Words: 50
Unique: 42 (84%)
Longest word: programming
Reading time: 1 min
Top words: python (3), easy (1), effectively (1)
```
steps.solution:
import math
words = get_words(TEXT)
counts = count_words(words)
print(f"Words: {len(words)}")
print(f"Unique: {len(counts)} ({round(unique_ratio(words) * 100)}%)")
print(f"Longest word: {max(words, key=len)}")
print(f"Reading time: {max(1, math.ceil(len(words) / 200))} min")
top = top_words(counts, 3, STOP_WORDS)
print("Top words: " + ", ".join(f"{w} ({c})" for w, c in top))

tests.stdout:
Words: 50
Unique: 42 (84%)
Longest word: programming
Reading time: 1 min
Top words: python (3), easy (1), effectively (1)

missions.finale: Paste in your own essay or an article (replace TEXT) and see what it says about your writing. This is the same counting idea search engines started with.

missions.title: Solo: Library System
missions.tagline: Design the classes for a lending library from a spec. Your structure, hidden tests.
missions.intro: **Solo project.** Real jobs start like this: a list of rules from someone who isn't a programmer, and a set of things the code must be able to do. Deciding which classes to make and what each one knows is the design part, and it's yours. Only the public interface below is fixed, because other code (the hidden tests) uses it.
missions.scaffold:
from datetime import date, timedelta

{{program}}

steps.title: Build the library
steps.text:
The library's rules:
- Books are identified by ISBN and can have several copies.
- Members borrow books for **14 days**. A member can hold at most **3 books** at once, and can't borrow a second copy of a book they already have.
- Members with an overdue book can't borrow anything until it's returned.

Make a class `Library` with exactly this interface (anything else is up to you, including extra classes):

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add_book(isbn, title, copies=1)` | add a book, or more copies of an existing one |
| `add_member(member_id, name)` | register a member |
| `checkout(member_id, isbn, day)` | lend a copy on `day` (a `date`); returns the due date |
| `return_book(member_id, isbn)` | give it back |
| `available(isbn)` | copies currently on the shelf |
| `books_of(member_id)` | titles the member holds, sorted |
| `overdue(today)` | `(member name, title)` pairs past their due date, sorted |

Raise `ValueError` with these exact messages when something isn't allowed: `unknown member`, `unknown book`, `no copies left`, `limit reached`, `already borrowed`, `has overdue books`, `not borrowed`.
steps.stub:
# Solo project: design it your way.
# Required: class Library with add_book, add_member, checkout, return_book,
# available, books_of and overdue (see the table).

tests.exec:
lib = Library()
lib.add_book("111", "Dune", copies=2)
lib.add_book("222", "Emma")
lib.add_book("111", "Dune")
lib.add_member("m1", "Ava")
assert lib.available("111") == 3 and lib.available("222") == 1, "Copies add up"
due = lib.checkout("m1", "111", date(2026, 10, 1))
assert due == date(2026, 10, 15), f"Due 14 days later, got {due}"
assert lib.available("111") == 2
assert lib.books_of("m1") == ["Dune"]
lib.return_book("m1", "111")
assert lib.available("111") == 3 and lib.books_of("m1") == []
tests.label: Lending and returning
The right error messages
The 3-book limit

tests.exec:
lib = Library()
lib.add_book("1", "Zorro"); lib.add_book("2", "Atlas"); lib.add_book("3", "Bee")
lib.add_member("a", "Ava"); lib.add_member("b", "Ben")
lib.checkout("b", "1", date(2026, 5, 1))
lib.checkout("a", "2", date(2026, 5, 1))
lib.checkout("a", "3", date(2026, 5, 10))
assert lib.overdue(date(2026, 5, 15)) == [], "Due on the 15th is not overdue on the 15th"
assert lib.overdue(date(2026, 5, 16)) == [("Ava", "Atlas"), ("Ben", "Zorro")]
try:
    lib.checkout("a", "1", date(2026, 5, 20))
except ValueError as e:
    assert str(e) in ("has overdue books", "no copies left"), str(e)
lib.add_book("4", "Cat")
try:
    lib.checkout("a", "4", date(2026, 5, 20))
except ValueError as e:
    assert str(e) == "has overdue books", f"Got {e}"
else:
    raise AssertionError("A member with an overdue book can't borrow")
tests.label: Due dates and overdue books

missions.finale: You turned rules into a design. Compare yours with a friend's: there are many good answers (one class or three, loans stored on members or on the library). Next: add reservations (a queue of members waiting for a book) and late fees.

missions.title: Solo: Meeting Scheduler
missions.tagline: The engine behind calendar apps. Rooms, conflicts and free time, fast enough for 20,000 meetings.
missions.intro: **Solo project.** Calendar apps answer two questions all day: *how many rooms do we need?* and *when is everyone free?* Both have slow obvious answers and fast clever ones. The hidden tests include a day with 20,000 meetings, so you'll need the patterns from the last unit (sorting, sweeping through events, heaps, merging intervals).
missions.scaffold: {{program}}

steps.title: The scheduler
steps.text:
Times are `"HH:MM"` strings on a 24-hour clock. A meeting is a `(start, end)` tuple. A meeting ending at 10:00 doesn't clash with one starting at 10:00.

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `rooms_needed(meetings)` | the smallest number of rooms that fits every meeting |
| `assign_rooms(meetings)` | a room number for each meeting, **in the input order**. Handle meetings by start time (ties: input order); each takes the **lowest-numbered** room that's free, and new rooms are numbered 1, 2, 3… |
| `common_free(calendars, day_start="09:00", day_end="17:00", length=30)` | `calendars` is a list of people's busy meetings. Return every window (as `("HH:MM", "HH:MM")`) inside the working day when **nobody** is busy, at least `length` minutes long, in order |

Example: `rooms_needed([("09:00", "10:00"), ("09:30", "11:00"), ("10:00", "10:30")])` is 2.
Tip: convert times to minutes first (`"09:30"` → 570), and back at the end.
steps.stub: # Solo project: write rooms_needed, assign_rooms and common_free.

tests.label: 20,000 meetings, quickly

missions.finale: These are real algorithms from real calendar products: a sweep over sorted events, a heap of free rooms, and merged intervals. Next: let people mark meetings as optional, or find the earliest slot where at least 3 of 4 people are free.

missions.title: Solo: Bank Statement Analyzer
missions.tagline: Turn a raw bank export into a monthly money report. No scaffolding.
missions.intro: **Solo project.** Your bank lets you download transactions as CSV. missions.title: Solo: Word Guessing Game
missions.tagline: A 5-letter word game from a blank file. You design it; hidden tests check it.
missions.intro:
**Solo projects have no scaffolding.** You get a description of what the program must do, an empty file, and hidden tests. How you structure it is up to you. This is what real programming feels like, and it's the skill that matters most.

Stuck? Break the problem into small functions, test each one with `print`, and use **Step** to watch your code run.
missions.scaffold: {{program}}

steps.title: The whole game
steps.text:
Build the classic 5-letter word game.

**1. Scoring.** Write `score(guess, answer)` that returns a 5-character string:
- `G` (green): right letter in the right spot
- `Y` (yellow): the letter is in the answer, but somewhere else
- `.`: not in the answer, **or** already used up by greens and earlier yellows

Repeated letters are the tricky part. `score("SPEED", "ABIDE")` is `..Y.Y`: ABIDE has only one E, so only the first E in SPEED turns yellow and the second gets a dot. Score greens first, then hand out yellows only while the answer still has that letter left over. Work in uppercase.

**2. The game.** Write `play(answer)`:
- ask with `input("Guess: ")`, turn it into uppercase
- not exactly 5 letters: print `Guesses must be 5 letters.` (it doesn't use up a try)
- otherwise print the guess, a space, and its score, e.g. `TOAST ..G.G`
- correct: print `Solved in N!` (N = valid guesses used)
- after 6 wrong guesses: print `Out of guesses. The word was PLANT.`

Finish with `ANSWER = "PLANT"` and `play(ANSWER)`. The Input box has some guesses to try.

missions.intro: A fractal is a shape made of smaller copies of itself. That makes recursion the perfect tool: build one piece, then call yourself to build the smaller pieces.

steps.title: A recursive tree
steps.text:
Write `tree(x, y, z, size)`:
- build a trunk of `"wood"`: a column of `size` blocks going up from (x, y, z)
- if `size` is 2 or less, put a `"leaves"` block on top and stop (base case)
- otherwise, from the top of the trunk, grow four smaller trees of size `size // 2`: one step out in each direction (x + 1, x − 1, z + 1, z − 1), each starting one block above the trunk's top
Skip any block that would land outside the world (x and z from 0 to 31, y below 24).

missions.title: Generate a World
missions.tagline: Hills, lakes, beaches and snowy peaks from a few lines of math.
missions.intro: Open-world games don't hand-place every hill. They generate terrain from math: a **height function** gives the ground level at each (x, z), and rules decide what goes where. That's procedural generation.

steps.title: A height function
steps.text:
Write `height(x, z)` that returns a whole number from 1 to 12 describing the ground level. Mix a few smooth waves so it looks natural:
`5 + 2.5 × sin(x / 4) + 2 × cos(z / 5) + 1.5 × sin((x + z) / 7)`, rounded, then clamped to 1–12.

tests.call: all(1 <= height(x, z) <= 12 for x in range(32) for z in range(32))

steps.title: Build the land
steps.text: Write `build_terrain()`: for every (x, z), fill a column from y = 0 up to `height(x, z)`. The top block is `"grass"` (or `"snow"` if the height is 10 or more, or `"sand"` if it's at most `SEA + 1`), the 2 blocks under it are `"dirt"`, and everything below is `"stone"`.

tests.exec:
clear()
build_terrain()
x, z = 0, 0
h = height(x, z)
assert get(x, h, z) == "grass" and get(x, h - 1, z) == "dirt" and get(x, 0, z) == "stone", "Grass on top, dirt under it, stone below"
peaks = [(x, z) for x in range(32) for z in range(32) if height(x, z) >= 10]
assert peaks and all(get(x, height(x, z), z) == "snow" for x, z in peaks), "Peaks of 10+ are snowy"
assert get(18, 1, 15) == "sand", "Low ground near the sea is sand"
tests.label: Layers of grass, dirt, stone, sand and snow

steps.title: Lakes
steps.text: Write `add_water()`: wherever the ground is lower than `SEA`, fill with `"water"` from just above the ground up to `SEA`.

tests.exec:
clear(); build_terrain(); add_water()
assert get(18, 2, 15) == "water" and get(18, SEA, 15) == "water" and get(18, SEA + 1, 15) is None, "Water fills low ground up to sea level"
tests.label: Low ground floods to sea level

steps.title: A forest
steps.text: Write `plant_trees(n)`: seed the random generator with `random.seed(3)`, then pick random (x, z) spots between 2 and 29 until you've planted n trees. Only plant on `"grass"` tops, and keep trees at least 3 blocks apart (track the spots you've used). Each tree is a 3-block `"wood"` trunk with `"leaves"` on top and on the 4 sides of the top trunk block.

assert len(trunks) == 30, f"10 trees × 3 trunk blocks = 30, found {len(trunks)}"

tests.label: Trees on grass only

missions.title: Build a Village
missions.tagline: Houses, towers and trees as classes. Make one, then make twenty.
missions.intro: When you need many similar things, write a class once and make as many objects as you like. Each building knows its own position and size, and how to build itself.

steps.title: A House class
steps.text:
Write `class House(x, z, width=6, depth=5, height=4, wall="planks", roof="brick")` with a `build()` method that:
- builds hollow walls from y = 1 to `height`: only the edge cells of the width × depth rectangle starting at (x, z)
- leaves a 1-wide, 2-tall doorway in the middle of the front wall (the z = z + depth − 1 side), at x = x + width // 2
- puts a flat `roof` layer covering the whole rectangle at y = height + 1

tests.exec:
clear()
House(2, 2).build()
assert get(2, 1, 2) == "planks" and get(7, 4, 6) == "planks", "Walls go around the edge, from y = 1 to 4"
assert get(4, 2, 4) is None, "The inside is hollow"
assert get(5, 1, 6) is None and get(5, 2, 6) is None and get(5, 3, 6) == "planks", "A 2-tall door in the front wall at x = 5"
assert get(4, 5, 4) == "brick", "A flat roof at y = height + 1"
tests.label: Hollow walls, a doorway and a roof

steps.title: A Tree class
steps.text: Write `class Tree(x, z, height=4)` with `build()`: a `"wood"` trunk from y = 1 to `height`, then a ball of `"leaves"` around the top: every cell within distance 2 of (x, height + 1, z), where distance is `abs(dx) + abs(dy) + abs(dz)`. Don't overwrite the trunk.

tests.exec:

Tree(10, 10).build()
assert get(10, 4, 10) == "wood" and get(10, 5, 10) == "leaves", "Trunk up to y = 4, leaves around y = 5"
assert get(12, 5, 10) == "leaves" and get(12, 6, 10) is None, "Leaves reach distance 2, no further"
tests.label: A trunk with a round crown

steps.title: Inheritance, a tower
steps.text: Write `class Tower(House)`: a square stone tower. Its `__init__(x, z, size=5, height=9)` calls `super().__init__` with `wall="stone"` and `roof="cobble"`. Override `build()` to call `super().build()` and then add battlements: a block on every other cell of the roof's edge, at y = height + 2.

assert isinstance(t, House) and t.wall == "stone", "A Tower is a House with stone walls"

tests.label: A tower with battlements

dojo.title: String compression
dojo.q: Write `compress(s)`: replace runs of the same character with the character and its count, `"aaabccdddd"` → `"a3b1c2d4"`. If that isn't shorter than the original, return the original.
dojo.solution:
def compress(s):
    out = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = i
        while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:
            j += 1
        out.append(s[i] + str(j - i))
        i = j
    result = "".join(out)
    return result if len(result) < len(s) else s

dojo.title: Product of the others
dojo.q: Write `products(nums)`: for each position, the product of every **other** number. No division allowed (there might be zeros). Use one pass from the left and one from the right.
dojo.solution:
def products(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

dojo.title: Spiral order
dojo.q: Write `spiral(grid)`: read the grid in a clockwise spiral starting at the top-left.
dojo.solution:
def spiral(grid):
    out = []
    g = [row[:] for row in grid]
    while g:
        out += g.pop(0)
        g = [list(r) for r in zip(*g)][::-1]
    return out

tests.exec:

dojo.solution:
def add_minutes(time, minutes):
    h, m = map(int, time.split(":"))
    total = (h * 60 + m + minutes) % (24 * 60)
    return f"{total // 60:02d}:{total % 60:02d}"

dojo.title: Password strength
dojo.q: Write `strength(pw)`: one point each for length ≥ 8, length ≥ 12, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit, and a symbol (anything else). Return `"weak"` for 0–2 points, `"ok"` for 3–4, `"strong"` for 5–6.
dojo.solution:
def strength(pw):
    points = sum([
        len(pw) >= 8,
        len(pw) >= 12,
        any(c.islower() for c in pw),
        any(c.isupper() for c in pw),
        any(c.isdigit() for c in pw),
        any(not c.isalnum() for c in pw),
    ])
    return "weak" if points <= 2 else "ok" if points <= 4 else "strong"

dojo.title: Settle up
dojo.q: After a trip, `balances` says how much each person is owed (positive) or owes (negative); they add up to 0. Write `settle(balances)` that returns a list of payments `(payer, receiver, amount)`: repeatedly have the person who owes the most pay the person owed the most, as much as possible, until everyone is at 0. Break ties alphabetically.
dojo.solution:
def settle(balances):
    bal = dict(balances)
    payments = []
    while True:
        payer = min(sorted(bal), key=lambda p: bal[p])
        receiver = max(sorted(bal), key=lambda p: bal[p])
        if bal[payer] >= -0.005:
            return payments
        amount = round(min(-bal[payer], bal[receiver]), 2)
        payments.append((payer, receiver, amount))
        bal[payer] += amount
        bal[receiver] -= amount

dojo.title: The sneaky side effect
dojo.q: `top_three(scores)` returns the right answer, but after calling it, the leaderboard elsewhere in the app is suddenly sorted differently. The AI's code changes the caller's list. Fix it so the original list is never touched.
dojo.solution:
def top_three(scores):
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:3]

dojo.title: Off by one page
dojo.q: Pages are numbered from **1** in the app. The AI's `page(items, number, size)` skips the first page entirely and returns an empty list for the last one. Fix it, and return `[]` for page numbers below 1.
dojo.start:

dojo.title: The midnight bug
dojo.q: `is_weekend(timestamp)` gets a UTC timestamp like `"2026-10-10T02:30:00+00:00"`, but the store runs on New York time (`STORE_TZ`, UTC−4 in October). The AI ignored time zones, so Friday-night orders count as Saturday. Convert to the store's time zone with `.astimezone(STORE_TZ)` before checking the day.
dojo.start:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

STORE_TZ = timezone(timedelta(hours=-4), "New York")

def is_weekend(timestamp):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(timestamp).weekday() >= 5
dojo.solution:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

STORE_TZ = timezone(timedelta(hours=-4), "New York")

def is_weekend(timestamp):
    local = datetime.fromisoformat(timestamp).astimezone(STORE_TZ)
    return local.weekday() >= 5
